articles.title_orig: California man’s smuggling scheme sent $300 million in AI hardware to China, feds say
articles.title_zh: California man’s smuggling scheme sent $300 million in AI hardware to China, feds say
articles.content_orig:
This is read by an automated voice. Please report any issues or inconsistencies here .
See more from the L.A. Times in Google Search. Set us as preferred
The owner of a San Gabriel Valley technology company was arrested Thursday after federal prosecutors charged him with smuggling more than $300 million of restricted computer hardware to China.
Greg Lui, the owner of Earthmade Computer Inc. in the City of Industry, allegedly sold high-end computer servers containing U.S.-manufactured Nvidia chips to the Chinese government, while claiming they were meant for customers in Malaysia and Singapore, according to the federal indictment filed  this week.
The U.S. Commerce Department doesn’t require an export license to ship this type of hardware to those two countries, but does for shipments to China.
“Protecting America’s national security means keeping our advanced Super Intelligence technology from being used to strengthen our adversaries’ military capabilities,” First Assistant U.S. Atty. Bill Essayli said in a Justice Department news release . “We will aggressively prosecute those who put our national security at risk for profit.”
The chipmaker’s graphics processing units, or GPUs, still dominate the artificial intelligence data center market. But the stock has tumbled 16% since hitting an all-time high on May 14.
President Trump signed an executive order this week rebranding “artificial intelligence” technology as “super intelligence” amid backlash and doomsday warnings about the rapidly developing tech — including from some AI executives .
Lui has been charged with one count of conspiracy to violate export controls, one count of outbound smuggling and one count of conspiracy to commit money laundering. An attorney representing him  has not yet been listed in available court documents, and The Times was unable to reach Lui for comment.
The federal indictment, filed Tuesday in the Central District of California, comes as some lawmakers have sought to curb tech exports to China, even as AI chip companies such as Nvidia and AMD lobby against restrictions.
Trump last year relaxed some export controls on advanced chips sold to China and, with his executive order this week, rebuffed calls for regulation of AI, saying it  would hamper economic growth and competition.
President Trump’s new national security strategy tempers U.S. support for longstanding allies and recasts U.S. global interests in business terms.
The indictment alleges Lui and his co-conspirators provided false documentation to chip manufacturers that showed the items would be going to users in  countries such as Malaysia and Singapore.  However, prosecutors say, Lui used  freight-forwarding companies to ship the high-end servers containing the microchips from Malaysia and Singapore on to China.
The indictment cites bank records and emails, including a purchase order to a U.S. manufacturer for 27 servers with Nvidia H100 chips for about $7.6 million. A packing list, the indictment said, showed they were shipped from the Los Angeles area to the Malaysian capital of Kuala Lumpur. But soon after, a co-conspirator of Lui’s allegedly emailed a Malaysian government official saying that all 27 were shipped to China.
In 2024, Earthmade received more than $176 million from two Malaysia-based shipment companies as part of the scheme, prosecutors said.
Among the chips Lui is accused of exporting to China are the Nvidia A100 and H100. While no longer the company’s most advanced chips, they are powerful enough to be used in AI applications. H100 is a somewhat newer chip released in 2022 that is optimized to handle large language models creating text, computer code, images, video and audio.
Demand for chips designed by Nvidia, a Santa Clara-based company, has ballooned dramatically amid the AI boom, and some lawmakers worry that access to the hardware could strengthen China’s bid for technological and military dominance and weaken the U.S.’s position.
Chuan Geng and Shiwei Yang, who owned and operated ALX Solutions Inc., were arrested on suspicion of illegally exporting “tens of millions” of dollars’ worth of microchips, authorities said.
After the U.S. placed chip-export controls on China in 2022, Nvidia designed less-powerful versions to access the market while complying with the rules. But those reduced-capability models were later  restricted too.
Late last year, Trump announced that he authorized Nvidia to sell its H200 chip in China in exchange for taking 25% of the revenue, although exports remain heavily restricted.
Last year, federal prosecutors similarly charged two Chinese nationals living in Southern California with illegally exporting tens of millions of dollars’ worth of artificial intelligence microchips to China.

articles.title_zh: New World Development Co Ltd (NWWDF) (H1 2026) Earnings Call Highlights: Hong Kong Sales Hit ...
articles.content_orig:
Sales in the first eight months of 2026 rise by 8.5 per cent compared with the same period last year
Hong Kong’s retail sales rose by 5.6 per cent year on year in August, with the latest figures showing consumer spending picking up after growth eased for two consecutive months.
Retail sales value reached HK$32 billion (US$4.1 billion), according to provisional figures released by the Census and Statistics Department on Friday. Sales in the first eight months of the year rose by 8.5 per cent compared with the same period in 2025.
“Growth was seen across many types of retail outlets, while online retail sales value grew notably, reflecting a continued shift in consumer spending towards digital channels,” a government spokesman said.
The latest figures followed a 4.5 per cent increase in July, when sales reached HK$31 billion, the lowest monthly value recorded in the first seven months of the year. Growth had slowed from 7.9 per cent in May to 4.6 per cent in June.

articles.title_orig: Lake of the Ozarks teen heads to China for wakesurfing competition
articles.title_zh: Lake of the Ozarks teen heads to China for wakesurfing competition
articles.content_orig:
A teenager from the Lake of the Ozarks will travel to China this month to compete in the 2026 IWWF World Wakesurf Championships.
Victoria Moroski, 17, is a three-time national champion and four-time Masters World champion in the WWA Wakeseries. She began wakesurfing at age 12 after a friend introduced her to the sport.
“I like to wakesurf a lot,” Moroski said. “I just like being outside and doing a lot of activities.”
Moroski said she fell in love with the sport after breaking her ankle and watching friends surf while she recovered.
“I think I fell in love with it when I broke my ankle and I had to watch everyone on the boat surf and I couldn’t do it for six months,” Moroski said.
“I was like, ‘Dang, I really want to do this.’ I think that’s when I really wanted to do it more.”
She began competing in tournaments three years ago.
“I thought it’d be really fun to compete,” Moroski said. “I like competing and trying to win trophies.”
But the trophies aren't the main reason she competes. Moroski said the real reward is the sense of accomplishment she gets from something she spends hours training for.
At 16, Moroski was selected as the best athlete in her division and joined Team USA Wakesurf.
Team USA will travel to Hangzhou, China, for the 2026 IWWF World Wakesurf Championships, scheduled for Oct. 9-17.
Moroski said athletes from 20 countries are expected to compete. It will be her first international competition.
“I’m super excited,” Moroski said. “I can’t wait to meet other surfers from different countries.”
To prepare for competitions, Moroski said she builds a routine around tricks she is confident performing and practices them repeatedly.
“I practice them over and over for hours until I get them,” Moroski said. “I’ll read my Bible, pray about it, and just stay really calm and try to do the best I know how to do.”
Her favorite trick is a 3-shuv, an aerial maneuver in which the rider pops the board out of the water and spins it 360 degrees beneath their feet before landing back on the board.
Moroski said her coaches, Whitley Stewart Roberts and Sean Silveria, and parents have been the most influential people in her wakesurfing career.
“Whitley’s the best female surfer in the world, and Sean was one of the best pro men surfers in the world,” Moroski said. “They are my coaches and teach me all my new stuff.”
Roberts is a four-time world champion, while Silveria is a one-time world champion wakesurfer and six-time world champion flowrider.
Silveria has trained several athletes, including Jett Lambert, who is described as one of the top wakesurfers in the world.
Moroski said training can be challenging, especially on days when things don’t go as planned on the water.
“Some days you have bad training days, and it makes you super frustrated,” Moroski said. “You just have to push through it.”
Moroski said wakesurfing is “really fun” and that she is excited to compete in China.
“I just can’t wait to meet everyone and make a lot of new friends there,” Moroski said.

articles.title_zh: Think Tank Director Reevaluates European Foreign Policy After US, China Threats
articles.content_orig:

Households in the contiguous United States will pay thousands of dollars more for energy through 2040 because of federal policy changes since President Donald Trump returned to office such as canceling new clean energy projects, according to modeling released Friday by a nonpartisan think tank.
The Energy Innovation analysis found that households will pay an average of $6,500 more for energy, cumulatively through 2040. In five states, households will pay roughly $9,000 more: Oregon , Mississippi, South Dakota, Virginia and Wyoming.
The California-based think tank said there will be more demand for natural gas for electricity because the administration is canceling new wind, solar and hydrogen projects and there will be more gasoline demand for transportation because Trump and Congress are revoking policies that incentivized efficient and lower-emissions vehicles. Higher demand increases prices.
Energy prices are elevated in many countries. The International Energy Agency said after Russia invaded Ukraine, record prices were observed between 2022 and 2024 in the European Union, the United Kingdom, Japan and Korea. In many countries, the rise has outpaced income growth and inflation since 2019, including the European Union and the United States.
In some areas of the U.S., demand from data centers is being blamed. The Iran war has sent oil and gasoline prices sharply higher, too. The Energy Information Administration expects residential U.S. customers to pay about 18.6 cents per kilowatt-hour in 2027, compared to 17.3 cents in 2025 and 18.2 cents in 2026.
The independent research firm Rhodium Group has also examined the issue, saying in April the U.S. has entered a new period of rising electricity prices. It cited increasing price volatility in natural gas, which is increasingly used to generate power; needed grid improvements; inflation; storm recovery and wildfire mitigation; and shifting policies.
Absent significant policy action, electricity prices likely will continue their significant rise over the next five years, the firm said.
White House spokeswoman Taylor Rogers said Wednesday that lowering electricity prices remains a top priority and Trump is unleashing reliable energy like coal and natural gas to reverse the damage Democrats did to the grid by increasing clean energy. A 2025 Department of Energy report, mandated by Trump, warned of increasing blackouts if the U.S. continued closing coal and natural gas plants.
“Joe Biden created a grid crisis; President Trump is fixing it,” Rogers wrote in an email. “If the Democrats had their way, these costly and unreliable renewable energy projects would still be failing our grid and our communities.”
The Republican president prioritizes fossil fuels to produce electricity, unlike Biden, who saw clean energy as a climate solution. The conservative Institute for Energy Research said in December that blue states have high rates because they have embraced aggressive renewable mandates, 100% carbon-free targets, premature coal and nuclear retirements and restrictions on natural gas infrastructure. It said high electricity prices are not an inevitability; they are a choice.
Analysis examined impact on states solely from federal policy changes
It focused on the sweeping package of tax breaks that slashed funding for clean energy tax credits, known as the One Big Beautiful Bill, Trump signed; environmental rollbacks, including clean air and power plant rules and the revocation of a scientific finding that underpinned the U.S. fight against climate change; the loosening of fuel economy standards and blocking of California’s novel rule banning the sale of new gas-powered cars by 2035; and federal actions to stop wind, solar and hydrogen projects.
These changes will result in annual household energy costs rising in every state in the contiguous U.S., plus job losses in 47 of 48 states and losses to the gross domestic product in 46 states, Energy Innovation said. It's projecting 37,000 additional premature deaths from air pollution, $72 billion in additional healthcare costs and more than 9 billion tons of additional carbon pollution because of the environmental rollbacks. The analysis did not include Alaska or Hawaii because key federal data is not available for those two states, said Robbie Orvis, senior director for modeling and analysis.
“Across pretty much every state, things are worse. The outlook now is worse for states and the affordability crisis will be worse because of the combined set of policies,” Orvis said.
Climate Justice Alliance legislative director Mar Zepeda said her Washington, D.C., electric bill increased $200 in the past month. Zepeda blames electricity demands from data centers, and said federal “affordability” policies only exacerbate this.
“They may call it affordability, but affordable for whom and at what cost? Not for regular people,” Zepeda said in an email.
White House says the think tank is partisan
Rogers said it is “irresponsible” to classify Energy Innovation as nonpartisan because its employees have donated to Democrats and worked with Democrats on climate policy.
Spokesman Silvio Marcacci said Energy Innovation works with policymakers who want to cut emissions and lower bills, regardless of party. He said multiple Republican-led states have used their tool designed to model policies affecting energy use and emissions. Much of their data comes from government sources, including the EIA.
Rogers also said states led by Democrats that have embraced aggressive renewable mandates see higher energy costs, notably California and New York. She said this proves Republican policies are working.
However, in the Energy Innovation analysis, three of the five states facing the highest costs have Republican governors. Its research has found that states with high levels of wind and solar generation, including Republican-led Iowa and Oklahoma, have experienced the lowest rate increases.
The average price residential customers pay for electricity increased during Biden's term and has continued to rise under Trump, according to EIA data.
Oregon households’ annual energy spending slated to increase the most
The modeling projects federal policy changes will increase annual energy spending in Oregon by $840 per household in 2035 and $1,200 per household in 2040, with a cumulative $9,300 increase from 2026 to 2040 — the highest of any state.
The Oregon Citizens’ Utility Board advocates for residential utility customers. Executive Director Bob Jenks called those numbers “frightening” because Oregon already has an energy affordability problem. He cited steep rate increases as utilities make upgrades and data centers use more power.
As costs rise, Jenks expects utilities to disconnect more customers who can't afford their bills.
Jenks said wind and solar are essential for affordable electricity, and he wants the federal government to partner with states to develop the energy they need.
“We're trying to optimize among the resource options we have, and they’re trying to take things away and raise the costs,” he said.

articles.title_orig: EXCLUSIVE: G7 countries agree on release of diesel and oil stocks after US pressure
articles.title_zh: EXCLUSIVE: G7 countries agree on release of diesel and oil stocks after US pressure
articles.content_orig:
This live page is now closed but you can read more in our news story
Leaders from the G7 bloc of advanced economies have agreed to work "in a coordinated manner" to help bring down diesel prices
They will make production "more flexible", release strategic reserves of "up to 100 million barrels" within four months, and avoid energy restrictions between partner countries
The meeting comes after President Donald Trump threatened to ban diesel exports - to bring US prices down - unless Europe agreed to release its reserves
Following the G7 announcement, Trump tells reporters at the White House : "We're not going to be doing the export ban"
Average UK diesel prices have hit a record high, according to motoring group the RAC , reaching Â£2 a litre for the first time
However, UK Transport Minister Keir Mather says Britain's supply of diesel is "robust" and "resilient" and the country has a wide range of sources
"I can barely afford to travel to work", says Kaine from Manchester , while Richard, from Buckinghamshire, says he's spending nearly Â£500 a month extra on fuel
Edited by Charlotte Hadfield and Tinshui Yeung
Leaders of the G7 nations have agreed to release up to 100 million barrels of oil and diesel in a bid to ease supply pressures that have caused prices to skyrocket.
It comes after diesel hit record highs in the UK, reaching Â£2 a litre for the first time ever, as conflict in the Middle East continues to push up the cost of fuel.
One worker, from Buckinghamshire, told the BBC he was spending an extra Â£500 a month on diesel as a result of the surging prices, while a charity said it may have to reduce aid shipments due to delivery costs.
US President Donald Trump, who has previously put pressure on Europe to release fuel reserves , warned he would ban US diesel exports if European countries did not agree to put more of their own stocks onto the market.
Following a meeting of G7 leaders, Trump told reporters outside the White House this evening that he would not impose the export ban, adding that Europe will be "making a major world contribution, and so are we".
In the UK, while diesel prices are at record levels, analysts say an actual shortage is highly unlikely, reports our business correspondent Theo Leggett .
We're ending our live coverage, but you can read more here:
The US president seems to have got his way, chief North America correspondent Gary O'Donaghue reports.
US President Donald Trump has said there will not be a US export ban on diesel.
It comes after he initially threatened to ban diesel exports - to bring US prices down - unless Europe agreed to release its fuel reserves.
Following a meeting of G7 leaders this afternoon, the group agreed to release 100 million barrels of their energy reserves to ease supply pressures that have caused prices to skyrocket.
Speaking to reporters at the White House this evening, Trump said: "We're not going to be doing the export ban", adding that Europe will be "making a major world contribution, and so are we".
Naj Modak BBC North West reporter
Rising diesel prices have left a family-run transport company paying about an extra Â£67,000 in fuel since the Iran conflict began in February.
British Blue Tours in Birkenhead on the Wirral, Merseyside, has also delayed adding an extra vehicle to their fleet to try and recoup the money.
The firm "would like more reassurances" that there will be no fuel shortage and it can continue to operate.
Traffic manager, Rob Jones, says: "Due to our work commitments and contracts, we're not able to recoup any sort of additional costs back from our customers."
"We do factor in fuel cost increases, but we just weren't expecting them to hit such highs," he says.
Jones adds that for a small family run business the "significant" hike in costs comes out of their profits.
"That's money that goes towards updating the fleet, which is why we've obviously had to push back on our new vehicle."
Adrian Peter says his customers are "stunned" by rising fuel prices
As fuel prices increase, people across Europe are also feeling the impact on their daily lives.
The manager of Peter & Krebs, a heating oil supplier in Berlin, says "people are stunned" by rising prices.
"Naturally, they try to negotiate every possible discount," Adrian Peter tells Reuters news agency. "But wholesale purchasing costs are extremely high, and we have no choice but to pass those costs on."
Peter says he's also noticing that many customers are no longer filling their tanks completely.
"Instead, they are only ordering enough to get by, opting for half-load deliveries or much smaller orders than usual," he explains.
A customer, Burkhard Seidler, comments: âTo be honest, it's an absolute shock. We're simply shocked. Why should 100 litres of heating oil cost 160 euros?â
Samira Hussain New York business correspondent
If you look in the US, we've been seeing record high diesel prices for the last couple of weeks - and if you compare today to this time last year, prices are up some 70%.
So the idea is that the G7 will start releasing some of that oil and - hopefully - it will bring down prices.
The Trump administration is looking at midterm elections about a month away now, and they're getting nervous because they are hearing from their constituents, and from their officials that are up for re-election, that the price of gasoline and the price of diesel is really high.
It's important to recognise the importance of diesel - as it's the fuel for business. Food production, for example, relies on those big tractors used on farms, which are fuelled by diesel.
And it is now costing farmers thousands of dollars more to fill up their vehicles.
The cascading impact is that food prices are going to get higher, and that's in addition to the inflationary pressures we've seen in the last few months.
Tom Espiner Business reporter
Diesel is used to power heavy machinery such as lorries, tractors, vans, boats and diggers.
It appeals to people such as lorry drivers, farmers and fishermen because it packs more punch than petrol and has more pulling power at lower speeds.
Farmers use red diesel, which is essentially diesel dyed red, as their main energy source , external . Itâs cheaper than road diesel because itâs taxed less.
The amount of diesel used in the UK rose between 1990 and 2025, while petrol use fell, according to the RAC Foundation , external .
Burning diesel generally produces more pollutants that affect human health.
Crude oil is a finite resource found in the Earthâs crust. It is a type of fossil fuel â the remains of organisms that lived and died millions of years ago.
Petrol and diesel are both produced from crude oil. One of the main differences between them is their boiling points. Petrolâs boiling point ranges from about 40C to 205C, while dieselâs is higher, generally at 160C to 350C.
Diesel is generally used in heavy vehicles because diesel engines provide greater low-speed torque and efficiency. Meanwhile, petrol engines may deliver higher peak power, which is why petrol is used in lighter vehicles.
According to the US Energy Information Administration, one barrel of oil, which is 42 gallons (159 litres), can produce about 19-20 gallons of petrol and 11-13 gallons of diesel.
Theo Leggett International business correspondent
Diesel prices are at record levels, but analysts say an actual
shortage is highly unlikely.
The UK has four refineries, which together produce about half of
what we use. The rest comes from abroad. Those refineries could produce more
diesel than they currently do - although imports would still be needed.
The UK also has stocks of gasoil, which includes diesel, that are
higher than this time last year. But if supplies do get tighter, whatâs
known as demand destruction comes into play.
Put simply, people will choose to travel less, because it costs
too much. That frees up supplies, because there is less demand. So the pumps
are unlikely to dry up.

articles.title_orig: Hollister teen to compete for Team USA at 2026 World Skate Games
articles.title_zh: Hollister teen to compete for Team USA at 2026 World Skate Games
articles.content_orig:
Dominic Rosales, a 16-year-old goaltender from Hollister, has been selected to represent Team USA's junior inline hockey team at the 2026 World Skate Games in Asunción, Paraguay, marking the biggest tournament of his career.
"I just want to, like, take the most out of it, experience how South America is going to be, having to represent Team USA. Play with my friends, you know, I think that will be the most I want to take out of it. Obviously, winning a gold medal would be cool too," Rosales said.
A gold medal would be a fitting achievement for Rosales, who has already proven himself as one of the nation's elite young goaltenders.
Rosales grew up watching his father, Diego, play as a goalie, inspiring him to pursue the position himself. His passion for the sport started early, even leading him to dress up as a goalie for Halloween.
"Me and my buddy just MacGyvered that thing. We just got a bunch of tape, cardboard, and hard foam, and we made his own little set. He was super happy. After Halloween, he used it every single day outside. He was able to slide across in the living room, and he thought he was the next goalie, you know? And it worked," Diego said.
Diego has been instrumental in supporting his son's dream, working three jobs over the years to ensure Dominic could pursue his passion for hockey.
"I think the most rewarding things out of this, sure, I'll take another job, another shift, do extra jobs here and there. I think the fact that he loves the sport makes it so much worth it, right? And we can look past all the rest of it," Diego said.
As Rosales prepares to compete on the world stage, he carries the pride of his hometown with him.
"It fills me with pride because I know Hollister will have my back and support me. They've been supporting me with this journey. I think, definitely coming back, I'll have a lot of pride. I'm happy I'm able to represent Hollister, a small town," Rosales said.

articles.title_orig: Christa Pike unconscious, on a ventilator at Nashville hospital, her lawyers say
articles.title_zh: Christa Pike unconscious, on a ventilator at Nashville hospital, her lawyers say
articles.content_orig:
Christa Pike, the woman who survived an execution attempt in Tennessee earlier this week, remains hospitalized in critical condition, her lawyers said in a new statement Friday.
She is unconscious, intubated and breathing through a ventilator. The death row inmate is also being treated for “significant injuries to both arms” sustained when two lethal injections of pentobarbital failed to kill her.
At one point, Pike said it felt like her arm was exploding, and she could be heard whimpering, according to her legal team.
“We are working closely with those closest to Christa to respect her wishes, safeguard her privacy and protect her rights as a patient during this extraordinarily difficult time,” attorney Luke Ihnen said in a statement. “We ask that the public and the media respect that privacy as well.”
The state of Tennessee attempted to put Pike to death Wednesday night by lethal injection for a murder she committed when she was 18.
Pike, now 50, has been on death row for decades and would have been the first woman executed in the state in 200 years.
NBC News earlier reported that there was no emergency medical oxygen in the execution room in case something went wrong. Medical professionals had to retrieve it from elsewhere.
Pike’s attorneys detailed her condition in a new emergency motion filed Friday asking the state to preserve all evidence from the failed execution attempt.
“In the words of one media witness: we have a lot of questions and the Department of Correction has a lot of answers that it needs to provide to the public about what happened here. We agree,” the motion reads.
In their filing, the lawyers described a painful and chaotic scene that unfolded in front of several witnesses, and that they said could have been prevented with the proper care and training.
Medical staff failed to follow basic protocol, like ensuring the needles used were fresh, functional and inserted properly, according to the motion. Further, the state did not heed Pike’s concerns prior to the procedure that preexisting medical conditions could make lethal injection difficult to complete, the motion says.
The motion accuses the department of corrections of “inflicting a cruel and unusual punishment on Ms. Pike through its deliberate indifference to her basic medical needs and reckless disregard of basic medical practices and their own lethal injection protocol.”
The Tennessee Attorney General did not immediately return a request for comment on the new filing. A spokesperson for the state department of corrections said the agency does not comment on pending litigation.
At a news conference Thursday, Stephen Ferrell and another of Pike’s attorneys, Randall Spivey, detailed how the execution attempt went wrong . Spivey, who was in the room, recalled Pike saying she was in pain, and like she felt like her arm was about to “explode.”
“It’s not supposed to be a cruel and an unusual execution,” criminologist Deborah Denno told NBC News. “The goal is to kill somebody, but to kill them within means or in a reasonable way, where there’s not going to be pain and suffering.”
According to Friday’s filing, the execution process lasted longer than two hours. Pike’s legal team filed emergency motions to halt the execution in multiple courts before the prison called an ambulance.
“Even then,” it continues, “attorneys for the State of Tennessee argued that TDOC had no obligation to render life-saving care to Ms. Pike.”
NBC News contributor Dr. Natalie Azar, a rheumatologist, said the pain Pike described could be attributed to pentobarbital flowing into her arm instead of straight into her veins. That would be painful with any medication, Azar said, but the specific properties of pentobarbital would make the experience exceptionally uncomfortable.
The scenario would also result in Pike being administered a less-than-lethal dose. It was enough to suppress her respiratory system but not enough to kill her, Azar explained. The question of how long Pike’s brain was deprived on oxygen will be central to her prognosis.
“There is no reversal of pentobarbital. There is no medicine or antidote,” she said. “You have to basically wait for the liver to metabolize the drug and get it out of your system.”
Pike was convicted in the 1995 murder case. She and two other teenage accomplices worked together to torture, slash and fatally beat Colleen Slemmer, Knoxville police said at the time. Pike was sentenced to death. A number of last-minute legal efforts to stop Pike’s execution were unsuccessful.

articles.title_orig: What to know about the Cornell University rape allegations
articles.title_zh: What to know about the Cornell University rape allegations
articles.content_orig:
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said Friday that a woman who alleges she was drugged and raped by multiple members of a Cornell University fraternity in 2024 was "failed" by those obligated to protect her.
Hochul's comments came a day after announcing she had lost faith in the district attorney overseeing the Cornell University rape case and signed an executive order appointing New York Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to lead the investigation.
"In what world would the police learn from a victim that she'd been literally gang raped while intoxicated by five men in a fraternity house and not elevate those allegations to the district attorney?" Hochul said at a press conference with James in New York. "In what world does the district attorney not even interview her or anyone else involved or even request the full transcript?
"At every turn, she was failed by people and institutions with an obligation to protect her," Hochul said.
James said that the case is "now an active criminal investigation."
"We will review the facts, gather evidence, interview witnesses and, if warranted, pursue prosecutions," James said, adding: "I know that you want answers. I do too."
Read more from Yahoo: A timeline of the Cornell rape case, from the alleged 2024 incident to the appointment of a special prosecutor to oversee the criminal investigation
New York Governor Kathy Hochul speaks during a news conference with New York Attorney General Letitia James in New York on Friday.
Tompkins County District Attorney Matthew Van Houten has come under intense scrutiny in recent days over his decision not to prosecute anyone when the initial allegations were made in 2024.
In a civil lawsuit filed last month against the school and seven current and former fraternity members, a former student identified as "Jane Doe" alleged that she was the victim of a "gang rape" at the Chi Phi fraternity on Cornell's Ithaca, N.Y., campus on Oct. 19, 2024. She said she was already intoxicated when she arrived and was given ketamine before and during the alleged assault. She reported the incident to campus police three weeks later.
Van Houten said earlier this week that Jane Doe's sworn statement to police didn't include allegations that she was "drugged against her will or gang raped."
"On the contrary, Jane Doe's statement described her participation in drug use and sexual conduct as voluntary, conscious, and consensual," Van Houten said. "My office obviously did not and could not have based our November 2024 decision on the allegations in a civil lawsuit that would not be filed until nearly two years later."
On Tuesday, CBS New York published excerpts from Jane Doe's Nov. 14, 2024, interview with Cornell police, in which she asserted, "I can say with 100% confidence I was raped."
"Shockingly, those words never made it into the account that the Cornell police sent to prosecutors," Hochul said Friday.
Van Houten said he was not provided with a transcript of her interview before his office decided not to pursue charges.
"I'm going to follow up on this because this is news to me," Van Houten told CBS. "If she had said those words, we certainly would want to have explored that more. Like I said, that wasn't provided to me."
Cornell University Police vehicles are seen on campus on Sept. 29.
According to ABC News , Jane Doe told the school's investigators that she "felt like bait" on the night of the alleged assault.
"I felt like lions around me," she said during a 2025 hearing. "It just was a totally debilitating place to be in."
The comments were included in a 99-page report prepared by the university as part of its Title IX investigation, per ABC.
The report also included comments from a fraternity member who Cornell's investigation concluded did not engage in the assault but was found responsible for "attempted sexual exploitation."
"I was sorry that maybe if it wasn't consensual and she was victimized, I was sorry for not stopping it," the fraternity members said, according to ABC.
Two of the men have released statements through their lawyers denying they participated in a sexual assault, according to the Associated Press.
Cornell University issued a statement pushing back against claims that the school did not thoroughly punish those involved in the alleged assault.
"Any suggestion that the university did not impose consequential punishments for those involved is false," the university said. "A continuation of the false narrative that there were minimal consequences in this case is irresponsible, will make survivors feel less safe and supported, and will perpetuate the underreporting of sexual assault."
Hochul announced on Wednesday that Cornell had agreed to initiate an independent review of its initial response to the allegations.
The governor also said she would work to close a loophole in New York law, which states that someone who was voluntarily intoxicated cannot claim they were mentally incapacitated during an assault, unless they can show they were "physically helpless" and unable to communicate consent.
"If someone is too intoxicated to consent, it should not matter whether they chose to use drugs or alcohol," Hochul said. "Voluntary intoxication is not a license for sexual assault or gang rape. Period."
The Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell University in Ithaca, N.Y., is seen on Sept. 28.
On Sept. 14, Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit against Cornell University and seven members of the Chi Phi fraternity, alleging that she was the victim of a "gang rape" at the fraternity house when she was incapable of consent — and that the school failed to protect her from "sexual predators" on its campus.
The defendants named in the lawsuit include Cornell, the seven fraternity members, the Chi Phi fraternity, the woman's own sorority, Delta Delta Delta, and an off-campus bar that allegedly served her alcohol.
She is seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages resulting from "sustained psychological injuries, severe emotional distress, along with pain and suffering and loss of enjoyment of life."
According to her lawsuit, Jane Doe was a 20-year-old student at the school in October 2024 when she went to visit a friend at the fraternity house on Cornell's Ithaca, N.Y., campus while intoxicated. Shortly after arriving, Jane Doe alleged that she was pressured by two fraternity brothers into snorting what they said was ketamine before sexually assaulting her. One of the men then allegedly sent a message to the fraternity's Snapchat group suggesting that she was available for sex. A screengrab of part of the chat was included in the lawsuit.
According to the complaint, multiple other members of the fraternity showed up, and she was raped for hours.
"The Snapchat was disgusting and vulgar and immoral," Van Houten told ABC News. "But the question that we analyzed was, did Jane Doe consent to what happened? And the law in New York state is clear: That if you are voluntarily intoxicated, or under the influence of drugs such that your judgment is impaired, that does not legally under the penal law constitute your inability to consent."
During the alleged assault, the fraternity members "began pouring lines of Ketamine all over her body and snorting them," according to the complaint.
"At around 5:45 AM, this assault concluded and Plaintiff lost consciousness," the lawsuit stated.
About three weeks later, on Nov. 8, 2024, Jane Doe reported the incident to the university's police department.
According to ABC News , Jane Doe told police in a sworn statement on Nov. 15, 2024, that the incident "felt like coercion," and that at one point she said "no to the foursome" one of the fraternity brothers had proposed. She also stated: "I felt like I was unable to make any decision because of how intoxicated I was."
According to the New York Times , she told Cornell's Title IX investigators that she did not consider herself a victim until she saw the incident being discussed in an online forum.

articles.title_orig: Shivon Zilis says she was 'let go' from relationship with Elon Musk
articles.title_zh: Shivon Zilis says she was 'let go' from relationship with Elon Musk
articles.content_orig:
By DANA KENNEDY, SENIOR INVESTIGATIVE REPORTER and EMILY CRANE
Published: 12:02 EDT, 2 October 2026 | Updated: 14:43 EDT, 2 October 2026
Elon Musk 's longtime love and baby mama Shivon Zilis has revealed the billionaire abruptly ended their relationship 'with no warning' - with the mom-of-four declaring 'it’s hard to go from in love to let go in a week.'
'Hurting' Zilis, an executive at Musk’s brain implant startup Neuralink, poured her heart out in a lengthy X post on Friday - just hours after eagle-eyed social media users noticed the billionaire had stopped following her on the platform he owns.
'I’ve loved him more than life itself and he’s taught me 100 lifetimes of knowledge and made my cup overflow with life meaning, so there is a lot of loss, but luckily we created four beautiful little loves of my life,' Zilis, 40, wrote on X.
'I am so beyond grateful for our children and they make every single day the best day of my life! I do hope and pray he and I can be great friends and coparents.'
Zilis, who is believed to have first embarked on a secret tryst with the Space X founder back in 2016, went on to describe Musk as a 'tortured soul.'
'I feel happy that I got to show Elon how it feels to be deeply understood, nurtured, and peacefully loved with stability and gentleness,' she wrote.
'I loved being that counterbalancing place of safety, sense of calm, and love - and delighted in bringing a smile back to his face when he was down. I will miss him dearly.'
Zilis - the mother of four of Musk's 14 kids - hinted, too, that she was blindsided by the breakup - sharing a screenshot of loved-up text messages the pair had exchanged just last week.
Elon Musk's longtime love and baby mama Shivon Zilis revealed on Friday the billionaire abruptly ended their relationship 'with no warning.' The couple are pictured back in February
Zilis and Musk have four children together, including twins Strider and Azure, who were born by IVF in November 2021
'It was really wonderful to see you for breakfast. Love you very much,' Zilis texted Musk.
'Love you too. I didn't realize that this Xi dinner included significant other (Beijing one did not) or I would have invited you,' he responded on September 24, referencing the White House state dinner for the Chinese president. Zilis replied: 'Aw, that means so much to me. Thank you.'
Musk, 55, hasn't yet commented on the breakup.
Zilis ended her post by saying: 'I’m hurting, but care deeply about E and will always be cheering for his happiness. God speed, Elon, the world is lucky to have you.'
The first apparent sign of trouble in the couple's romance came back on September 28 when Zilis had posted a cryptic message on social media: 'New day, new life.'
Then, earlier on Friday, Big Tech Alert, an account that tracks the online activity of technology figures, flagged that Musk had unfollowed her.
The Tesla founder only follows around 1,400 accounts.
News of the shock split comes just months after Zilis - who is one of four women Musk has children with - took the stand as a key witness in the Space X founder’s case against OpenAI earlier this year.
Zilis, who is the mother of four of Musk's 14 kids, hinted she was blindsided by the breakup - sharing a screenshot of loved-up text messages the pair had exchanged just last week
Zilis, who is the mother of four of Musk's 14 kids, hinted she was blindsided by the breakup. They are pictured in February last year meeting Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi in Washington, DC
Zilis and Musk, pictured with their eldest children, embarked on a romantic relationship in 2016. When Zilis decided she wanted to have kids as a single mom, Musk 'offered to make a donation' as a platonic sperm donor towards the end of 2020
It was during her testimony that key details about their once-secret romance were laid bare.
Zilis, who was born in Ontario, Canada and studied at Yale University, had first met Musk through OpenAI - the artificial intelligence lab he co-founded in 2015.
She testified that their relationship began as 'a one-off' at a corporate off-site event - but later turned romantic around 2016.
Zilis told the jury that when she decided to have children as a single mom, Musk 'offered to make a donation' as a platonic sperm donor towards the end of 2020.
Their twins, Strider and Azure, were born by IVF in November 2021. News of their third child, Arcadia, surfaced in June 2024. And their son, Seldon Lycurgus, followed in February 2025.
Zilis testified that she lives in a house in Austin, Texas where Musk often stays when he visits their children.
Zilis and Musk have brought their children to various White House events  in recent years. They are pictured in February 2025
Musk, for his part, called Zilis his 'partner' when it was his turn to testify.
The couple were spotted holding hands as they arrived at the wedding of White House deputy chief of staff Dan Scavino at President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate back in February.
Prior to becoming director of operations and special projects at Neuralink, Zilis had previously worked as a project director on Tesla's Autopilot team from 2017 to 2019.
In the wake of their split, it wasn't immediately clear whether Zilis would keep her roles at Neuralink and Musk's other companies.
The Daily Mail has reached out to Zilis and Musk.

articles.title_orig: Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max AT&T Glitch Requires Device Replacements
articles.title_zh: Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max AT&T Glitch Requires Device Replacements
articles.content_orig:
Getting your Trinity Audio player ready...
UPDATE: Apple has confirmed a problem affecting the AT&T iPhone 18 Pro Max.
"We have identified an issue affecting a small number of iPhone 18 Pro Max users on the AT&T network that may cause a device to lose service and be unable to make calls," Apple tells 9to5Mac . "We released iOS 27.0.1 earlier this week and strongly encourage all iPhone 18 Pro Max users to update now, and are also issuing a carrier settings update today. These updates together are meant to help prevent this issue from occurring.”
The update is intended to prevent this from happening to other phones, 9to5Mac notes. If your iPhone has already lost service, you'll need to take it in to be replaced.
Original Story: Ever since the iPhone 18 Pro Max launched last month, AT&T customers have complained about being unable to make calls, send texts, or use cellular data. According to MacRumors , the carrier acknowledged the issue in a text message to customers this week and recommended an immediate software upgrade to fix the issue.
“Hi, it’s AT&T. Action needed: An important Apple software update for your iPhone 18 Pro Max is available. Some phones may be unable to complete calls/text/data, including to 911. Update to iOS 27.0.1 immediately,” reads AT&T’s message to customers.
Apple's iOS 27.0.1 began rolling out to iPhone users on Monday. The release notes mention patches for a Face ID bug and camera-zooming issues on iPhone 18 Pro models, as well as a fix for an unresponsive screen issue . No mention of AT&T issues, though.
Even after updating to iOS 27.0.1, cellular issues persist for some AT&T customers. "I cannot make or receive cellular phone calls on the brand-new phone I set up this morning," Lindsay Robertson, a writer and editor from Brooklyn, tells PCMag. "Nor can I make or receive them on my old phone. AT&T, you have ONE JOB!"
Robertson now plans to visit the AT&T store this weekend to re-activate her old phone before going to the Apple Store to get a replacement iPhone 18 Pro Max. "I will just have to pray that all that work fixed it," she says. "I spent over two hours talking to AT&T support this morning, with each minute becoming more infuriating."
It's unclear whether the issue lies with the carrier or the iPhone hardware. Neither Apple nor AT&T has explained the cause. If you want to try your luck, you can update your iPhone software by going to Settings > General > Software Update.
An AT&T spokesperson tells us that the Apple update should "address an issue that may affect calls, data, texts, and 911 calls on a small number of Apple iPhone 18 Pro Max phones," adding, "Our top priority is ensuring customers can stay connected when they need it most, and we are working with Apple to make it right.”
On Apple’s Community forum , we spotted a few customers saying they visited an Apple Store, where staff ordered replacement units for them. Some have already received their new phones and say the AT&T connectivity issue has been resolved. Most of those comments were posted before Monday's iOS 27.0.1 update, so we have reached out to Apple for more details.
Editors' Note: This story was updated with comments from AT&T and Robertson.
Jibin is a tech news writer based out of Ahmedabad, India. Previously, he served as the editor of iGeeksBlog and is a self-proclaimed tech enthusiast who loves breaking down complex information for a broader audience.

articles.title_orig: Another disappointing jobs report suggests more challenges for Trump, GOP
articles.title_zh: Another disappointing jobs report suggests more challenges for Trump, GOP
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. economy created far fewer jobs than expected in September, pointing to a surprising soft spot in the labor market and broader economy.
Nonfarm payrolls rose a seasonally adjusted 29,000 for the month while the unemployment rate increased to 4.2%, the Bureau of Labor Statistics reported Friday. Economists surveyed by Dow Jones had been looking for job growth of 84,000 and an unemployment rate of 4.1%.
In addition to the weakness in September, the August jobs count was revised lower to reflect a gain of 133,000 while July switched from a gain to a loss as payrolls fell by 10,000. The revisions in total showed 60,000 fewer jobs than previously reported.
Market reaction was swift to the report, with traders interpreting the soft jobs numbers as good news as they likely further cemented the Federal Reserve staying put at its October meeting.
Stock futures rose sharply after the release while Treasury yields slumped after recently rising to levels not seen since the early part of the century. Market-implied odds that the Fed will hold rates steady at its Oct. 27-28 meeting jumped to 82.8%, according to the CME Group's FedWatch tool.
"For the Fed, this number should be the nail in the coffin for an October hike," Thomas Simons, chief U.S. economist at Jefferies, said in a note.
"The payroll data surged in August, and we had expected the momentum to continue this month, given the historically low prints on jobless claims in recent weeks," he added. "However, it now appears that the August number was nothing more than a rebound from very weak hiring in June and July."
Fed officials more closely watch the unemployment rate than the headline payrolls numbers.
The household survey, which is used to calculate the jobless level, was considerably better than the establishment survey, which is used to derive the payrolls count.
Household employment rose by 406,000 for the month, while the labor force swelled by 485,000 and the participation rate, which counts those working or actively searching for a job as a share of the total labor force, increased 0.2 percentage point to 61.8%, its highest since May.
An alternative measure of unemployment, which includes discouraged workers and those holding part-time jobs for economic reasons, edged down to 7.6%, its lowest since January 2025.
The report comes with Federal Reserve officials weighing the state of the economy and how it should affect their next interest rate move.
Following statements in recent days from central bank policymakers, markets have recalibrated expectations and now expect the rate-setting Federal Open Market Committee to hold off until December for its next hike. The FOMC raised benchmark rates a quarter percentage point in September.
Policymakers largely see inflation as a larger threat to the economy than the labor market, which had shown resilience in recent months. The data has painted a picture of a low-hire, low-fire economy, with weekly jobless claims low and one indicator showing layoffs at their lowest rate in four years.
Inflation, though, has held well above the Fed's 2% target. The most recent indicator of the central bank's preferred gauge showed core inflation at a 3% annual rate.
Wages, though, continued to show signs of disinflation.
Average hourly earnings increased just 0.1% in September, putting the 12-month gain at 3%, the lowest since May 2021. Wall Street had been looking for readings of 0.3% and 3.1%, respectively. The average work week was unchanged at 34.6 hours.
"Americans are frustrated by the lack of opportunities right now," said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union. "Wage growth fell to a new 5-year low and is being wiped out entirely by inflation. That stings heading into the holidays."
However, Long described the labor market as "stable" and said she doesn't think the Fed will be dissuaded from hiking in December.
Most of the monthly job gains came from healthcare, which added 17,000 workers. Construction was up by 11,000, and manufacturing added 9,000.
Government employment fell by 17,000, while temporary help services saw a decline of 11,000, and information services lost 10,000 amid worries over the impact artificial intelligence may have on the jobs picture. Financial activities also saw a drop of 7,000 jobs.
The weak job growth comes despite signs of strength elsewhere.
On a macro level, economic growth has been strong.
Earlier this week, the Commerce Department revised its count of both first- and second-quarter gross domestic product growth, to 2.5% and 2.2%, respectively. The Atlanta Fed is tracking third-quarter GDP at 3.7%.

articles.title_orig: As fires rage in Borneo, several of the world’s rarest primates are continually threatened
articles.title_zh: As fires rage in Borneo, several of the world’s rarest primates are continually threatened
articles.content_orig:
A nonprofit environmental group working with primates in Sebangau National Park says the dry peatlands can be a catalyst to more destruction.
(CN) â Since early August, wildfires have devastated the fragile rainforests of Borneo and Sumatra, causing widespread toxic air across Indonesia. Itâs affected most communities in all parts of the region of Kalimantan, a part of the worldâs third largest island under Indonesiaâs governance.
The fires are fueled by shifting El NiÃ±o climate patterns, causing severe drought and extremely dry conditions in the islandâs peatlands, among the planetâs most effective carbon-capturing ecosystems and vital habitat for wildlife found nowhere else in the world.
Sebangau National Park in Central Kalimantan is home to an estimated 6,000 to 9,000 critically endangered Bornean orangutans, one of the islandâs largest populations. The nonprofit Borneo Nature Foundation said a fire crossed the park boundary for the first time in early September.
âOur teams pushed it back, and it was largely confined to sedge and open peat, but some reforestation sites are impacted,â Dr. Susan Cheyne, the Science Director for the Borneo Nature Foundation and the Vice Chair for the International Union for the Conservation of Nature special project group for small apes, said in an email to Courthouse News.
âOur priority is to keep fire out of the forest, because that protects every orangutan in it at once,â she said. Cheyne and her colleagues monitor and document conditions in Borneo, while volunteer firefighting crews work to keep fires out of orangutan habitat and nearby villages. Capturing and removing the apes is âa last resort,â Cheyne said.
Sebangau is also home to several of the worldâs rarest primates, including the largest known population of Bornean white-bearded gibbons, an ape Cheyne has studied for over 20 years.
Gibbons are known for their musical vocalizations, or âsongs.â Males sing alone in the morning before females join them in duets later in the day.
âDuring the 2006 fires I found that gibbons sang less often and sang shorter songs on smoky days. Their song is how they defend territory and keep pair bonds, so this matters,â said Cheyne. âA similar pattern has since been recorded in wild Bornean orangutans exposed to wildfire smoke.â
Gibbons rarely come to the ground, and fire survivors are often left in small, isolated forest patches with little food. Other primates, including red langurs and long-tailed and southern pig-tailed macaques, are found only in Southeast Asia, and each fire further reduces their numbers. Little is known about how fires affect nocturnal slow lorises and western tarsiers, Cheyne said.
The national park includes vast peat swamps, made of partly decomposed plant material accumulated over thousands of years. In parts of Sebangau, the peat dome reaches 12 meters deep.
Peatlands are naturally waterlogged, like giant sponges that do not burn. But in the 1990s and early 2000s, illegal loggers dug hundreds of canals to float timber out of the forest. Those canals continue draining the peat, causing it to dry out and become fuel.
âIn a long dry season like this one, a dried-out peat swamp is a tinderbox,â said Cheyne.
âWhat makes peat fires so hard to fight is that they burn downwards and sideways, not just across the surface. Fire smolders underground through the dry peat, sometimes for weeks, long after the flames above have gone out. These are sometimes called zombie fires.â
Peat fires are particularly dangerous because from the surface, a person may see nothing amiss, perhaps âjust a thin wisp of smoke,â Cheyne said, while a meter below the peat burns and can set nearby tree roots aflame, easily toppling them. And peat fires also produce dense, toxic smoke.
Cheyne said since 2015, the foundation and local crews have built over 1,000 dams to block drainage canals, planted almost a million trees, drilled hundreds of water boreholes, and increased support for up to eight fire teams.
âThat preparation is why we are holding,â she said. But itâs still a tenuous situation. For the short-term, Cheyne said, the goal is to keep the firefighting teams in the field fed, equipped and safe, which costs about $100 a day per team. It also means investing in equipment, such as thermal drones that can detect underground peat fires and rewetting the peat, so it doesnât reignite. The foundation, she said, is actively seeking donations from international bodies, advocacy groups and concerned individuals.
While hotspots in Kalimantan have declined since the beginning of the month, according to the foundation, rains are not expected until late October or November.
âWe are not out of this yet,â said Cheyne.
Cheyne said Borneo Nature Foundation Internationalâs co-founder Simon Husson recently passed a troop of monkeys on a river trip and they moved through trees beside mile after mile of burned riverbank.
âThat is the picture,â she said. âLife hanging on right at the edge.â

articles.title_orig: FAA Says 737 MAX Software Glitch Doesn’t Pose Safety Issue
articles.title_zh: FAA Says 737 MAX Software Glitch Doesn’t Pose Safety Issue
articles.content_orig:
The Federal Aviation Administration said Friday that it has determined a new software glitch on some Boeing 737 Max aircraft isn't a flight-safety issue.
The determination paves the way to certification for the last model in the company's best-selling family of airplanes, the 737 Max 10, just as Boeing seeking to sell and deliver more aircraft after years of safety and manufacturing crises.
Boeing flagged the software issue, which could affect certain landing procedures, last month and the FAA on Monday said it was reviewing to determine if it poses a safety of flight issue.
"Following a thorough review, a panel of FAA safety experts on Friday determined a software issue in certain Boeing 737 MAX flight computers is not a safety concern," the FAA said. "The FAA's Corrective Action Review Board made that determination because pilots retain full control of the aircraft and the indications to the flight crew are clear and unambiguous."
Boeing said the issue could arise after a missed approach when pilots alter a preprogrammed flight path, and that pilots must take additional steps to use automated tools on subsequent approaches.
The FAA said on Friday that it will issue a special bulletin to airlines on how to recognize and respond to the issue if it arises.
The agency convened a review board on Friday to assess the issue. Participants included FAA experts on airframes, flight controls, propulsion, flight testing and others.
"As with any situation, the FAA will consider appropriate action if it receives new information about this issue," the agency said.
U.S. airlines said they're not affected by the issue since they could revert to older versions of the software, but the problem raised questions about certification of the Boeing 737 Max 10, which Boeing and airlines expected to come in early fall.
The Max 10 is the largest in the family of airplanes and would be the last of the Max lineup to win government certification to fly. The FAA approved the Max 7 , the smallest in the Max family, in August.
Chief executives of 737 Max 10 customers, Alaska Airlines and Ryanair, earlier this week brushed off concerns about the aircraft's certification delays.

articles.title_orig: Wayzata Sophomore Prepares to Represent Team USA at World Karate Championships
articles.title_zh: Wayzata Sophomore Prepares to Represent Team USA at World Karate Championships
articles.content_orig:
High school students face no shortage of challenges, from maintaining top grades to balancing extracurricular activities. But for Wayzata High School sophomore Aakya Manamperi, her pursuits extend far beyond the classroom. In fact, they stretch all the way across the globe.
Manamperi, 15, is a second-degree black belt and one of the nation’s top-ranked karate competitors in her age group.
Later this fall, she will travel to Spain to compete on the global stage at the World Karate Commission (WKC) World Championships.
Inside Dojo Karate in Medina, Manamperi serves as a patient instructor, guiding young students through fundamental martial arts skills. But don’t let her calm demeanor fool you. When she steps onto the tournament floor, she’s a force to be reckoned with.
“It’s kind of a really male-dominated sport,” Manamperi said. “So, being a female, and a female of color, it’s really important for me to go out there and represent.”
Aakya Manamperi teaches karate to a group of kids at Dojo Karate in Medina.
Manamperi began practicing karate at age 6. Achieving elite national status has required years of rigorous discipline and daily training.
“I’ve been training two hours every single day,” Manamperi said. “The first hour is mostly cardio, training drills, working on technique. And the second hour is just focusing on my kata that I’m going to be competing.”
Kata, her primary discipline, consists of detailed, high-intensity sequences of movements. Judges evaluate performance based on technique, power, rhythm, balance and presentation—an evaluation process that has earned Manamperi an impressive collection of trophies and medals over the years.
Her dedication has drawn praise from local mentors, including Dojo Karate Medina owner Javier Franco, who noted the positive influence she has on younger students.
“Of course, this is a big impact on the students,” Franco said. “They always see their instructors as their heroes.”
A collection of some of the awards Aakya Manamperi has received for her karate expertise.
Manamperi’s drive to make an impact extends beyond martial arts competition. Outside the dojo, she founded The Girl Shield Project , a student-led organization dedicated to empowering young women through self-defense training, leadership development and health education.
“We do online events, we do in-person events, and so far we’ve reached around 200 different girls in around 20 different countries, and hopefully growing to some more,” Manamperi said.
In addition to her athletic and community achievements, Manamperi maintains a 3.99 GPA at Wayzata High School, where she participates in Science Olympiad and Student Council.
As she prepares to represent the United States in Spain, the weight of her accomplishments is not lost on her.
“Honestly, I appreciate it so much,” Manamperi said. “It’s amazing for me to be able to share things that I like to do and my passions with the world and kind of compete in it. It’s something that I still pinch myself to this day about.”

articles.title_orig: China a better influence in Latin America than US: poll
articles.title_zh: China a better influence in Latin America than US: poll
articles.content_orig:
China is perceived more positively as a global influence than the United States in Latin America, according to a new regional survey, in a first since the poll began in 1995.
The 2026 Latinobarometro survey published on Friday found that 65 percent of respondents in 17 countries saw China as a positive influence. That was compared with 57 percent who said the same of the US.
Support for China has risen sharply since 2020, when 48 percent of respondents viewed its influence positively. The figure for the US has fallen from 60 percent over the same period.
Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic were the only countries surveyed where respondents viewed US influence more positively than China’s.
Latinobarometro, a Chile-based nonprofit organisation, conducts annual surveys across the region on issues including democracy, the economy, security and migration.
The findings come during US President Donald Trump’s second term, as his administration has sought to strengthen Washington’s influence in Latin America, particularly through exercising more military might.
That has included conducting strikes on alleged drug smuggling boats in the region, which rights groups have decried as extrajudicial killings, and abducting Venezuela’s then-leader Nicolas Maduro in Brazil.
Trump has described his approach as the “ Donroe Doctrine ”.
Despite the findings on global influence, the US remained more popular than China when respondents were asked about their overall views of the two countries.
Some 63 percent of respondents said they had a favourable opinion of the US, compared with 58 percent for China. The US figure was down from 73 percent in 2024.
The survey also asked respondents about the US military capture of Maduro .
A majority in all but one country, Argentina, approved of Maduro’s capture by US forces.
Views were more divided over what the operation meant for Venezuela, with 35 percent saying removing Maduro had benefitted the country and 28 percent saying it had harmed it.
Venezuelans were among the populations most likely to view US influence positively, according to the survey.
The 2026 survey was based on about 19,200 face-to-face interviews conducted in 17 countries between May 7 and June 17, with a margin of error of 1 percent.

articles.title_orig: Extreme Heat in Los Angeles Area Expected to Last at Least a Week
articles.title_zh: Extreme Heat in Los Angeles Area Expected to Last at Least a Week
articles.content_orig:
The seasonal pools are closed. Many playground fountains have been turned off. Along Southern California’s beaches, some lifeguard towers are no longer staffed.
But extreme heat is not. Forecasters say a dangerous heat wave is descending across much of Southern California, which is likely to bring triple-digit temperatures that will last at least a week.
Hot weather is not unusual in Southern California in October, but typically it lasts two or three days. The extended stretch of extreme heat makes this episode particularly dangerous, experts say.
October also tends to be one of the months when the risk of wildfires in Southern California is high because the vegetation has dried out after the summer and winds can grow stronger.
The wildfire risk will be elevated, particularly in inland valleys and mountains, but it is not expected to be so extreme as to prompt red-flag warnings.
Extreme heat warnings have been issued from Santa Barbara to San Diego, lasting through at least next Friday. Temperatures in downtown Los Angeles could reach 100 or higher on Saturday and Sunday, according to the National Weather Service. A few miles from downtown, the Dodgers are set to open a playoff series on Saturday in the middle of the day.

articles.title_orig: Hawaii's iconic 500-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch has collapsed into the sea
articles.title_zh: Hawaii's iconic 500-year-old Hōlei Sea Arch has collapsed into the sea
articles.content_orig:
Hawaii's famous Hōlei Sea Arch, a 90-foot-tall (27.4m) lava rock structure that formed about 550 years ago, has collapsed into the Pacific Ocean.
The collapse's exact time is not known. The arch was still projecting into the water from the coast of Volcanoes National Park on 23 September, but was gone by 27 September, the National Park Service (NPS) said.
"The coastline flanking the sea arch has shown signs of instability for years," NPS, which warned in 2021 that the arch would eventually crumble, said in a statement.
Located at the end of Chain of Craters Road on the island of Hawaii, also called "the big island", the formation was a popular - and heavily photographed - tourist destination.
The arch is believed to have fallen when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo last weekend.
The park service said earthquakes during the 2018 Kīlauea volcano eruption and summit collapse had damaged the cliffs near the arch.
Its ultimate collapse marks "the latest transformation of the park's remote and rugged coastline".
In January 2020, new cracks and instability in the cliffs led the park to close the original arch viewing area, and a few months later, a new viewing area opened at a safer distance, NPS said.
Waves from a tropical storm later that year broke off a chunk of rock from the bottom of the arch.
"This formation is beautiful, but temporary, and has a limited life span," the park service said in 2021. "The sea arch will eventually crumble into the sea. However, others will replace it as the cliff slowly migrates inland."
Thousands of people have liked and commented on the NPS social media post about the arch's collapse, including sharing their memories of visiting the arch and posting photos of it.
"Nothing and no one is here forever," one Facebook user commented. "Millions of years from now the sun will die. Appreciate the good, the beauty, now."

articles.title_orig: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.title_zh: Uzbekistan dominates chess Olympiad while England’s Sivanandan, 11, sets new world age record
articles.content_orig:
Host nation won having led almost from start to finish, while young English player reached a stunning landmark
Uzbekistan, the host nation, won the open gold medals at the 2026 Olympiad, the biennial chess international team tournament, at Samarkand last week in the style of the legendary Soviet grandmasters of long ago. India, the defending champions, were second, Germany a surprise third, and the top-seeded United States fourth.
The hosts led almost from start to finish, with world No 5 Nodirbek Abdusattorov and the world title challenger Javokhir Sindarov their top-board powerhouses. The team recovered swiftly from a single defeat by Germany, and were particularly impressive in crushing Armenia by 3.5-0.5 in the penultimate round. The Uzbekistan government rewarded each of the five players with $200,000 (£178,000), a house and a Volkswagen, plus $50,000 for the coach Rustam Kasimdzhanov.
India performed in line with their seeding. Putting the world champion, Gukesh Dommaraju, on board four boosted his results but also underlined that Sindarov is the favourite for the coming world championship match. Gukesh was exposed in the final rounds when he was outplayed against both Germany, although he won that game fortuitously, and Hungary.
The final leading scores were: Uzbekistan 20/22 match points; India and Germany 18 ; USA, Azerbaijan, Armenia and Hungary 17 ; China, France, Spain, Ukraine and England 16 (206 teams competed).
England’s creditable 12th place, one below their seeding, would have been higher still if a third player had performed at the level of the nine-time British champion Michael Adams, 54, and the Spectator chess columnist Luke McShane, 42, who were both in contention for individual medals right up to the final round. England’s women were 15th against their seeding of 20th, and the combined performance was the best since at least 2018, and probably since 1990.
Russia/USSR, which monopolised Olympiad golds in the second half of the 20th century, have been banned from the last three competitions due to the invasion of Ukraine. If allowed to take part, a team of Ian Nepomniachtchi, Andrey Esipenko, Daniil Dubov, Vladislav Artemiev and Alexander Grischuk would have been contenders.
The potential of Turkey’s Yagiz Kaan Erdogmus stands out. The 15-year-old won the individual silver medal unbeaten and has advanced to No 17 in the live ratings, a similar level to Bobby Fischer at that age and well ahead of current world No 1 Carlsen when he was 15. Here he defeats a rival prodigy , Argentina’s Faustino Oro.
China won the women’s Olympiad ahead of Kazakhstan, India and the US, and did so with its B team. World champion Ju Wenjun, world No 1 Hou Yifan, former title challenger Tan Zhongyi and world No 3 Lei Tingjie all stayed at home, but their substitutes, led by world No 4 Zhu Jiner and 16-year-old Lu Miaoyi, proved highly effective.
For the future, the US is potentially a powerhouse in women’s chess. Its duo of Carissa Yip, 23, and Alice Lee, 16, are both targeting the open GM title and its $100,000 bonus offered by Dr Jeanne Cairns Sinquefield, while new candidates are emerging in Rachael Li, Rose Atwell and Zoey Tang who are all teenagers with 2300+ ratings.
Bodhana Sivanandan broke the world age record for the youngest ever woman grandmaster (WGM). Her 8/11 total, playing all games with no rest days, included six wins, draws against Ukraine’s reigning European champion Anastasiia Hnatyshyn and Georgia’s former World Blitz champion Nana Dzagnidze, both of them current world top 20 players, and a solitary loss to Deysi Cori of Peru due to a time-pressure blunder in a drawn ending.
The 11-year-old Harrow schoolgirl’s record as the youngest ever WGM broke Hou’s 2006 mark by several months, and she also recorded her second norm (of three needed) for the international master (IM) title at open level. For IM, she also needs a 2400 rating against her current 2382, which includes the Olympiad.
Her last-round Olympiad game was a model of what has become her trademark style of a Magnus Carlsen grind.
If she secures her final norm and becomes an IM before her 12th birthday, she will break the all-time female No 1 Judit Polgar’s world age record and also become one of the 10 youngest ever IMs. She is already No 2 among all players born in 2015, behind only Russia’s IM Roman Shogdzhiev, who has been groomed for several years as a potential heir to Anatoly Karpov.
after newsletter promotion
The Guardian’s Matthew Weaver interviewed Sivanandan after her return home. At the end of the Olympiad the youngster talked with Lichess.org’s Theo Wait , while chess.com also covered her achievements in detail .
The Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport’s new £250,000 a year Supporting Elite Chess Fund document contains no specific provision for rewarding world-record breakers. Maybe it should, as Sivanandan’s IM title and new record could follow as soon as the London Classic, which begins in November.
Sivanandan has just started at secondary school, and that could slow her progress on the chessboard. The advance from IM to GM is difficult, and many talents eventually plateau, which should temper extrapolations of a rise comparable to Polgar and Hou.
Meanwhile Timur Turlov, 38, a Russian-born entrepreneur from Kazakhstan whose company Freedom Holding has a multibillion dollar valuation on the Nasdaq index, was elected as the new president of the world chess body Fide last Saturday.
The previous Fide President, Russia’s Arkady Dvorkovich, had planned to run for a third term but was forced to withdraw due to EU sanctions on his assets and travel visas.
Turlov received 96 votes against 76 for the German businessman Wadim Rosenstein and a surprisingly low 20 for the ticket of Jan Henric Buettner of Freestyle Chess and the ECF’s international director Malcolm Pein. In the run-off ballot they switched to Turlov, who defeated Rosenstein 110-85.
Turlov is young, committed and with proven business skills. However, there could be an immediate problem since Rosenstein has appealed to the court of arbitration for sport over the new president’s eligibility.

articles.title_orig: Gypsy Rose Blanchard's partner found dead in apparent drug-related incident - ABC News
articles.title_zh: Gypsy Rose Blanchard's partner found dead in apparent drug-related incident - ABC News
articles.source: Breaking News, Latest News and Videos
articles.content_orig:
"You will always be my greatest love story," Blanchard wrote on social media.
Gypsy Rose Blanchard 's partner Kenan Urker was found dead on his 34th birthday in what officials describe as an apparent drug-related incident, authorities said.
Officers discovered Urker dead when they responded to a call from a home in Raceland, Louisiana, on Thursday evening, according to the Lafourche Parish Sheriff's Office.
Urker, who was lying on a bed, was cold and his face and arms were blue, according to the sheriff's office. A paper towel on his arm appeared to have "blotches of blood" on it, the sheriff's office said.
On the nightstand next to the bed was a holstered handgun, a syringe and two shot glasses, according to the sheriff's office.
In the bathroom, deputies discovered syringes, a spoon and a "brown powdery substance," the sheriff's office said.
The sheriff's office said there's "no evidence of foul play."
Blanchard wrote on Instagram on Friday, "You will always be my greatest love story. You will be remembered and loved forever."
She added in an Instagram story that he was an "amazing father" and "will forever be my soulmate."
In 2015, Blanchard and her then-boyfriend Nicholas Godejohn were arrested for the fatal stabbing of Blanchard's mother, Clauddinnea "Dee Dee" Blanchard.
Gypsy Rose Blanchard pleaded guilty to second-degree murder and was released from prison in 2023 .
"Dee Dee" Blanchard had allegedly abused her daughter for years by convincing Gypsy Rose and the public that she was extremely sick, when she wasn't. "Dee Dee" Blanchard allegedly portrayed her daughter as a frail, disabled child who suffered from multiple illnesses including leukemia and muscular dystrophy, subjecting her to a life in a wheelchair, a feeding tube and unnecessary surgeries.
After her release from prison, Gypsy Rose Blanchard told ABC News she wanted to share her story "to bring awareness to mental health issues, to Munchausen by proxy, to abuse victims."
She said she hoped her story would serve as a "cautionary tale" for others.
"So that the next person that might be in a situation like mine, they don't take the route that I did," she said.
