articles.title_orig: The gambling world at war
articles.title_zh: The gambling world at war
articles.content_orig:
This week’s annual G2e conference in Las Vegas opened with American Gaming Association CEO Bill Miller telling the main stage audience his organization is “operating on war-time footing” in response to the wildfire growth of prediction market betting.
Miller’s opening was followed by more prediction talk during a “state of gaming” panel featuring MGM CEO Bill Hornbuckle, Caesars CEO Tom Reeg and Wynn CEO Craig Billings.
InGame’s Jill Dorson has G2e coverage here and more here .
Prediction markets have hit a cold streak in the courts of late, losing an appellate decision last week in the 6th Circuit, home to Ohio and Tennessee. That followed a loss in the 9th Circuit, which includes California, Nevada and Arizona, the last of which intends to push for a shutdown . The 4th Circuit is considering a case stemming from attempts to shut Kalshi down in Maryland.
There also was movement in New York, where the state sued Polymarket for running an illegal gambling operation. It took similar action against Kalshi in July.
As a practical matter, actions taken in legalized sports betting states will have less impact than those taken in populous states that haven’t legalized, since the latter is the unplowed land on which operators are competing for new customers. None of those states have moved against Kalshi since the rulings.
The other important development was on the regulatory front, where the CFTC proposed rule changes that would close a loophole that might have allowed for contracts around casino games such as blackjack and roulette, reinforced the Trump administration’s core argument that event contracts are swaps.

articles.title_orig: WebRTC Has Been a Boon
articles.title_zh: WebRTC Has Been a Boon
articles.content_orig:
Update your browser to view this website correctly. Update my browser now
Home › News and Business › News Makers
This is one in a series about how stations are creating and managing their audio from anywhere, thanks to virtualization, cloud, IP and other technologies. This is from the free ebook “ Audio Production (From Anywhere) .”
Jeff McGinley is vice president of engineering at SummitMedia . He says the company approaches distributed workflows in several ways.
“We have a remote morning show co-anchor in another state who uses a traditional codec to dial back into the station every weekday morning — tried and true and well-tested tech that’s been around forever,” he said.
“In three of our markets, we’ve upgraded studios to the Axia Altus console, which has a webRTC backend that allows any computer to act as if it’s a hardware codec.”
SummitMedia also has a remote studio in Gatlinburg, Tenn., located in a restaurant. It is used every week to dial back into the Knoxville stations for a live broadcast.
“Finally, we use the RCS Zetta2Go remote application if we have staff go to do a more traditional appearance remote. Our jocks can record a break on their phone a few minutes before the break is supposed to air. It gets sent to that market’s server, ingested and then played out as ‘almost-live.’”
For McGinley, the introduction of webRTC was crucial.
[Related: “The Stream Is as Important as the Transmitter”]
“This technology is going to change quite a bit in the next few years, and absolutely was not something that was available or at least on most people’s radar five to 10 years ago,” he said.
“Anyone with a laptop can connect via a VPN to the station network and broadcast from anywhere using a very basic setup. I believe that this is going to affect more than just broadcasting from anywhere, but how companies look at real estate and actual studio space,” he said.
“There is no need for a full-sized studio that requires HVAC and sound dampening. Anyone from anywhere with a decent mic and processor can be anywhere in the world and send audio back to get on the air, be it live for a specific on-air show or record a production bit for a commercial for a client.”
Can a complex multi-host morning show be executed as easily and smoothly via a distributed architecture as the traditional single-site installation?
“Absolutely. We are currently doing it with a traditional Comrex codec with a morning show that originates in Omaha but is distributed to almost 50 radio stations,” McGinley replied.
“One of our hosts moved to Pennsylvania, which is when we started doing this. However, this technology has been around for quite a bit now. I set up something similar with a morning show in Audacy in Seattle.”
The main concern, he said, is making the show sound like everyone is still in the same room.
“Kevin and Bean did this for years on KROQ-FM. The back-and-forth banter of the hosts that makes the show work needs to be paramount, even if they’re over 1,100 miles away from each other.”
Investing in IT infrastructure should be the first thing a company tackles when planning such an arrangement.
“On the top of your list should be a top-tier firewall, VPN tunnels and people who understand how to configure and maintain it. This is not something to skimp on.
“Thankfully at SummitMedia, we have the best IT person I’ve ever worked with, Brett Glover. All the credit needs to go to him. He is an absolute wizard at keeping everything running smoothly, keeping all of our VPN tunnels up and running. We also have a number of STLs through what Brett has accomplished.”
McGinley recommends that you conduct frequent penetration testing and educate staff through videos, emails and guidance about when to report suspicious material.
Looking ahead, “There is technology coming that will have both the automation system and a virtual console that will be cloud-based,” he said.
“There are still some considerations that haven’t been answered, like how satellite content delivery and closures will be addressed, but this will definitely be something that we broadcast engineers will have to get ready to deploy in the next few years.
“A wise man I know once said, ‘Wake up and smell the radio.’ Stay tuned. It’s only going to accelerate from here.”

articles.title_orig: NASA Has Been So Thoroughly Screwed by Boeing's Disastrous Starliner That It's Now Throwing Its Entire Access to Space Into Question
articles.title_zh: NASA Has Been So Thoroughly Screwed by Boeing's Disastrous Starliner That It's Now Throwing Its Entire Access to Space Into Question
articles.content_orig:
By all accounts, Boeing’s Starliner spacecraft has been nothing short of a disaster . It’s cost NASA a staggering amount of money, and even after over a decade of development, the capsule still has yet to complete a crewed mission to the International Space Station.
It’s been a humiliating saga, including a failed uncrewed launch attempt that went haywire thanks to a glitching computer, an aborted mission which stranded two NASA astronauts on board the station for nine months, and a litany of technical headaches along the way.
But now that SpaceX is threatening to retire its Crew Dragon spacecraft, NASA could soon be forced to make the plagued spacecraft work whether it likes to or not — while also calling into question its entire access to space.
“I do not think it’s a secret that SpaceX intends to sunset older platforms like Falcon and Dragon as they concentrate on their next-generation capability, Starship,” NASA administrator Jared Isaacman told reporters on Monday.
The agency said that it was weighing the option of buying two additional launches on Boeing’s Starliner.
Without SpaceX’s workhorse Crew Dragon spacecraft, which has regularly delivered crews to the ISS for six years now, NASA’s options could soon run thin. Starliner, which has cost Boeing billions of dollars, came eerily close to getting the axe altogether in 2024, but with SpaceX threatening to abandon its existing launch platforms in favor of its enormous and still unproven Starship, the space agency seemingly saw the writing on the wall.
NASA is also now stuck with the bill. The agency announced this week that it will commit $359 million to bail out Boeing and help it rebuild its reaction control system thrusters, arguably the biggest source of the spacecraft’s woes during its last, ill-fated mission.
The space agency will also need to certify the United Launch Alliance’s Vulcan rocket for crewed missions ahead of the retirement of the Atlas V.
The goal is to launch Starliner no earlier than December of this year. NASA also already has three pre-existing contracts for crewed missions with Boeing, per Ars Technica .
“We are starting with an uncrewed Starliner-1 mission to the International Space Station to validate the improvements made to the spacecraft and gather the flight data we need,” Isaacman said in a statement . “From there, we will use what we learn, continue implementing the corrective actions identified by our Program Investigation Team, and complete the testing and certification required for crewed flight.”
“Our current plan is to return astronauts on Starliner-2 by 2028,” he added.
It’s an awkward transitional moment for the agency. The ISS is set to be retired by the end of this decade, leaving a glaring hole in access to our planet’s orbit. It’s still unclear what will eventually replace the aging orbital outpost, with multiple private companies vying for lucrative government contracts to launch their own habitats.
If it were up to NASA, Boeing’s Starliner would probably be part of that vision — but given what we’ve seen so far, it’s anything but guaranteed.

articles.title_orig: A Cross-Border Problem: Modeling New World Screwworm’s South American Range
articles.title_zh: A Cross-Border Problem: Modeling New World Screwworm’s South American Range
articles.content_orig:
Traumatic myiasis is about as gross as it gets.
A gravid New World screwworm fly ( Cochliomyia hominivorax ) lumbers through the air, looking for the perfect place to deposit her heavy burden of eggs—maybe an open wound or an exposed mucus membrane. Eventually, they’ll hatch out tiny maggots, each sporting a treacherous spiral of backwards-facing spines. These will anchor the maggots as they use razor-sharp mouth hooks to burrow and tear into tender living tissue.
Historically, New World screwworm has been considered a livestock issue, affecting domesticated animals like cattle, sheep, and goats. But a wide range of warm-blooded animals can be hosts—including wildlife, household pets, and even humans.
That’s one takeaway from a recent study, published in August in the Journal of Medical Entomology , that applied a One Health approach to modeling New World screwworm distribution across South America. The team comprised disease experts, data analysts, entomologists, and veterinarians from institutions in Chile, Paraguay, and Venezuela.
“We all knew the fly affects livestock, but as we went through the literature, we came across cases in wildlife, such as maned wolves, giant otters, ocelots, lesser grisons, and wild boars,” says lead author Marlon Mauricio Ardila, a Ph.D. student at Chile’s Universidad de Concepción. “And that’s when you grasp the real problem. Those wild populations are completely outside the reach of any veterinary control, so they act as a reservoir that can keep the cycle going—even when you think you’ve already brought the fly under control in livestock.”
New World screwworm once affected a large swath of the Americas, from the southern United States through central Argentina. A program utilizing the sterile insect technique began in the 1950s and continued through the turn of the century to eradicate the fly in the U.S., Mexico, and central America. But it has returned to Central America in the past couple of years, reaching the U.S. this summer. All the while, populations remained strong in South America. But co-author Leidi Herrera of the Universidad Nacional de Asunción, Paraguay, and the Universidad Central de Venezuela says population data was limited.
“My research into metaxenic diseases and zoonoses … revealed significant gaps in surveillance in our region,” she says. “Although screwworm myiasis has a severe impact on health and the economy in Latin America, studies in South America were scarce.”
Existing models mainly looked at Argentina and Chile plus some nation-level analysis in some other South American countries. Now, the team wanted to model the distribution of New World screwworm for the entire region, with a strong focus on finding environmental conditions that might lead the flies to persist or disperse.
To do this, they used modeling tools along with records of New World screwworm myiasis cases in humans and other warm-blooded animals across nine geographic areas. The data included cases of more than 9,000 New World screwworm larvae, which broke out to about 38% involving human myiasis and nearly 62% involving non-human animals or unspecified myiasis.
This ecological modeling found that temperature and rainfall heavily influence the distribution of New World screwworm in South America—especially winter thermal stress. It turns out screwworm larvae and pupae don’t do well when the temperature dips to its lowest seasonal extreme. They also struggle when the temperature during the day is unstable, which is known to affect how well insects do normal things like fly, mate, and lay eggs.
The models also predict that some places—like the humid lowlands of eastern Paraguay, northeastern Brazil, and parts of the Amazon basin—have exactly what New World screwworm need to thrive: sufficient moisture so their pupae don’t dry out and plenty of opportunities for the flies to find vulnerable (and ostensibly tasty) wounds.
The team used epidemiological records to confirm and extend the models.
Overall, the team say that this problem is one that combines issues of the environment, animal health, and public health—and therefore requires an integrated approach to surveilling and responding to the threat.
“This is a starting point, not the end,” says Ardila. “For now, the paper calls for strengthening surveillance, training producers, and coordinating control across countries—because this is a cross-border problem.”
It also leaves many questions still open: confirming how wildlife act as a reservoir, figuring out the genetic barrier that prevents the flies from taking up areas that seem perfect from a climate perspective, and looking at how other flies that cause myiasis overlap New World screwworm . Herrera says they’re seeking partnerships and funding to design integrated monitoring tools and control strategies.
One thing is certain: It’s work that needs to be done together.
“ Presence and distribution of Cochliomyia hominivorax (Diptera: Calliphoridae) in South America: ecological niche modeling and epidemiological implications under the One Health approach ”

articles.title_orig: Connoisseurs Series Brings World-Class Artists to Southern Miss
articles.title_zh: Connoisseurs Series Brings World-Class Artists to Southern Miss
articles.content_orig:
Fri,
                     								10/02/2026 - 10:28am | By: Mike Lopinto
The University of Southern Mississippi’s School of Music will bring internationally acclaimed artists, distinctive musical voices and free
                     performances to Hattiesburg through its 2026-27 Connoisseurs Series. The series opens Oct. 27 at 7:30 p.m. in Marsh Auditorium with “A Centennial Celebration
                     of Miles Davis and John Coltrane.” The year 2026 marks the 100th birthday of the two
                     iconic artists in the world of jazz. The influence of Miles Davis and John Coltrane
                     was so pervasive that they reshaped the direction of the music for all who came after. The concert features New Orleans trumpeter Ashlin Parker and the Larry Panella Jazz
                     Quartet with Dr. Sam Bruton on piano, bassist Dr. David Pellow and Nathan Sanders
                     on drums. New Orleans jazz trumpeter Ashlin Parker is a nationally and internationally acclaimed
                     performer, educator and bandleader. Parker, a Grammy Award-winning musician with the
                     New Orleans Jazz Orchestra, has performed and recorded with jazz legends including
                     Ellis Marsalis, Terence Blanchard, Jason Marsalis, Herlin Riley, Nicholas Payton,
                     Kermit Ruffins, Dee Dee Bridgewater and Aretha Franklin. His international career
                     spans major festivals and tours across Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia, South America
                     and beyond. He leads the acclaimed Trumpet Mafia and serves as a professor of jazz
                     trumpet at the University of New Orleans, where he has taught since 2011. “Connoisseurs is about bringing exceptional artists and experiences to Southern Miss
                     while giving our students and community opportunities they simply might not encounter
                     anywhere else,” said Dr. Colin McKenzie, director of the School of Music. “This season
                     moves across musical traditions and styles, but every performance has the same goal:
                     to surprise, challenge and inspire.” The Connoisseurs Series showcases the breadth of the School of Music through guest
                     artists representing brass, woodwinds, strings, piano and voice. These artists complement
                     the work of Southern Miss’ nationally recognized faculty while giving students the
                     opportunity to learn directly from leading performers and educators. Four additional highlights of the 2026-27 season include: Cavatina Duo — Jan. 21, 2027, 7:30 p.m., Marsh Auditorium Spanish flutist Eugenia Moliner and Bosnian guitarist Denis Azabagić form the internationally
                     celebrated Cavatina Duo, praised for its virtuosity, expressive depth and remarkable
                     musical chemistry. The duo has performed throughout the world and earned acclaim from
                     Gramophone and other leading music publications. Dunamis in Concert, “An Evolutionary Journey through Gospel Music” — Jan. 28, 2027,
                        7:30 p.m., The Thomas V. Fraschillo Stage at the Mannoni Performing Arts Center Dunamis is an auditioned gospel ensemble at the Alabama School of the Arts, consisting
                     of 12 talented student vocalists and six mentor vocalists who are leaders, faculty
                     or staff members. The group’s name, Dunamis, derives from the Greek word meaning power
                     or strength, as referenced in Acts 1:8, which speaks of receiving power through the
                     Holy Spirit. Under the direction of Kenneth Brandon, Dunamis focuses on the rich heritage
                     and unmistakable sound of gospel music, celebrating Christ's nature through an extraordinary
                     demonstration of culture. Carter Johnson, piano — March 23, 2027, 7:30 p.m., Marsh Auditorium An award-winning Canadian concert pianist celebrated for his warm stage presence and
                     imaginative programming, Johnson received widespread international recognition as
                     the first Canadian finalist in the prestigious 2025 Van Cliburn International Piano
                     Competition, as well as the winner of the 2025 Dublin International Piano Competition.
                     He holds a bachelor’s degree in music from the University of British Columbia, a master’s
                     degree in music from Juilliard and a master’s degree in musical arts from Yale University,
                     where he is a doctoral candidate. Southern Miss Brass Symposium featuring Boston Brass — April 30-May 1, 2027, Bennett
                        Auditorium The renowned Boston Brass will headline a two-day celebration of brass performance
                     and pedagogy featuring clinics, master classes, performances and student chamber ensemble
                     showcases. The symposium is designed for performers, educators and anyone who appreciates
                     exceptional brass playing. All Connoisseurs Series performances are free and open to the public, made possible
                     through the support of The Arts Endowment, Bob and Judy Mixon, Mr. and Mrs. James
                     Simrall Jr., the Dr. John McLeod III and Bebe McLeod Endowment in the Arts, the Nan
                     and Ben Stevens Art and Music Endowment, the Robert N. Kinnaird Jr. and Lucille Ehlers
                     Kinnaird Memorial and Partners for the Arts. For more information about the Connoisseurs Series and other School of Music performances,
                     visit the School of Music website .
About the School of Music The School of Music at The University of Southern Mississippi is the state’s flagship music program and
                        a destination campus for the study of music across the region, the United States and
                        the world. Housed within the College of Arts and Sciences , the school offers bachelor’s, master’s and doctoral degrees and has earned a national
                        and international reputation for excellence. Its distinguished faculty members are
                        active performers and educators who appear on stages from local communities to major
                        international venues. The School of Music is home to acclaimed band, choral, orchestral,
                        jazz, opera and musical theater ensembles and provides extensive solo and chamber
                        music performance opportunities. Students regularly perform at regional, national
                        and international events and work with leading guest artists in preparation for careers
                        as 21st century performers and educators.

articles.title_orig: Picture of Jane Doe shared in Snapchat group on night of alleged Cornell rape
articles.title_zh: Picture of Jane Doe shared in Snapchat group on night of alleged Cornell rape
articles.content_orig:
Editor's warning: Some of the details in this story are graphic.
Chi Phi fraternity members shared a photo of the alleged victim in the Cornell University gang rape on Snapchat the night of the alleged assault, according to social media images obtained by CBS News.
In the photo, obtained through Jane Doe's attorney, she appears to be smiling with another man.
The photo was shared in a Snapchat group with dozens of Chi Phi fraternity brothers on the night Jane Doe was allegedly assaulted at the Chi Phi fraternity house at Cornell in October 2024.
Just before the photo was sent, one man wrote, "Like you can walk in and whip it out."
Right after the photo, someone in the chat asked, "Shop still open?" Another responded, "Yeah."
The alleged victim in the case, identified only as a then-20-year-old Jane Doe, has sued seven Cornell students and the university.
Two of the accused in the case were expelled, two suspended for at least two semesters, one had already graduated before any punishment could be handed down, and two were found not to be responsible for sexual misconduct, Cornell President Michael I. Kotlikoff said on Sept. 29. No one was arrested.
Two of those accused have denied responsibility through their lawyers.  Others have not shared statements.
The Tompkins County, New York, district attorney who decided not to press charges announced last month he was reopening the case in the wake of the lawsuit. Then on Thursday, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul appointed Attorney General Letitia James as a special prosecutor to replace Van Houten amid criticism over how the case was handled.
CBS News has obtained the findings of Cornell University's monthslong Title IX investigation into what happened that night. At a university hearing in May 2025, the then-sophomore said she "felt like bait" on the night of the alleged attack. She added, "I felt like lions around me. It just was a totally debilitating place to be in."
According to the report, she told campus investigators she took the drug ketamine and described it as feeling like the "lights are on, but nobody's home. Your brain is not functioning at its proper level."
CBS News New York also obtained hundreds of pages of interviews with Jane Doe, 20 witnesses and six of the seven men named in the lawsuit. In them, the men and Jane Doe share conflicting accounts of what happened.
Some of those men stated Jane Doe didn't appear to be intoxicated and that she gave consent. But Jane Doe describes a night that turned to horror, with multiple men coming in and out the room, stating at one point she felt "cornered," saying she "was a sex doll for all intents and purposes."
Later that night, she said was ushered into a closet by two of the men, calling it the worst experience she had the whole night, saying, "It was just raping." She said she was in and out of consciousness.
According to the Title IX investigation, one student who had been at the frat house the night of the alleged assault said she got a call the next day from one of the accused men who asked her to make sure a friend of hers didn't "say anything that she thinks might've happened last night."
In the days after the alleged assault, Jane Doe said three men apologized to her.
According to a transcript of her interview with campus investigators, she said she collected evidence, including the dress she wore that night. Two days after the alleged sexual assault, she went to a campus clinic to treat a urinary tract infection, according to her lawsuit.
Her attorney says she told doctors it was contracted in a "traumatic way," and instead of being referred for a rape kit, she was advised to "speak with somebody."
On Thursday night in a fiery town hall , Cornell students demanded change.
"Survivors need to know that when they come forward with their stories, somebody will listen and a broader institution will act upon it. Through this event, we have witnessed the complete opposite," said Jane Wang of the Cornell American Civil Liberties Union chapter.

articles.title_orig: Weak jobs report is yet another headwind for Trump and Republicans ahead of midterms
articles.title_zh: Weak jobs report is yet another headwind for Trump and Republicans ahead of midterms
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
September's weak jobs report was the last reading on the labor market before the midterm elections, and the weak figures will further complicate the job facing President Trump and Republicans to sell voters on their economic record.
The president and his party have already been grappling with an economic message that is failing to gain traction, as polls show voters are deeply unhappy about the economic trajectory one month out from Election Day.
US payrolls rose by just 29,000 jobs in September after 90,000 had been expected. Wage growth also cooled, another significant figure underscoring Americans' worries about their purchasing power amid persistent inflation.
Average hourly earnings rose just 0.1% in September and are up 3% over the entire year. That's below the 3.4% rate of inflation over that same period.
Friday's release also showed that the unemployment rate ticked up to 4.2%, and July and August payroll numbers were revised downward, further clouding the economic picture.
Read more: Credit card vs. savings: What to use when you're unemployed
Allianz chief economic adviser Mohamed El-Erian told Yahoo Finance on Friday that economic pressures have a pronounced effect on lower-income households.
"It's not just an economic worry. It's a social and political worry as well," El-Erian said.
Democrats were quick to tout the number as an indictment of Trump's economic record, while the White House and Republicans highlighted specific facets of the report to paint a more positive picture.
National Economic Council Director Kevin Hassett said in television interviews that he was "not even a little bit" disappointed by the number and that the US economy was being realigned. He acknowledged that the latest number was a "little bit lukewarm," but said that monthly job figures "bounce up and down."
Hassett and other White House officials, like Deputy Press Secretary Taylor Rogers, also focused on increasing labor force participation and pointed out that the government shed 17,000 jobs last month as private payrolls gained 46,000, although that latter figure was still below expectations.
Rogers noted that over 1 million private-sector jobs have now been created during Trump's second term.
Trump, meanwhile, continued to tout his economic message Friday, posting about investments from South Korea (even amid questions about whether South Korea was actually on board with the plan ).
The president is set to crisscross the country in the coming weeks to sell his economic record.
His message, as the election enters its final stretch to Nov. 3, is that the economy is in a "golden age" and the main issue is that he and his fellow Republicans have "done a very bad job of explaining."
Democrats, meanwhile, put the number in election-year terms. Sen. Elizabeth Warren of Massachusetts calculated that Trump's economy has added an average of 33,000 jobs a month since Inauguration Day in 2025 — "far below the 120,000-a-month average in 2024" of the last year of former President Joe Biden's time in office, she said.
Like other Democrats, Warren also zeroed in on weak wage growth, writing that "since the start of Trump's war [in Iran], real wages have fallen."
Gbenga Ajilore, chief economist at the Center on Budget and Policy Priorities and a former Biden administration official, added that "this is an okay reading for the labor market, but in the broader context, lower wage growth is a warning sign given the administration's harmful policies."
The latest release also comes as countless polls have shown Trump and Republicans deeply underwater on the economy, an area of intense focus among voters . A compilation of recent polls from Silver Bulletin shows an aggregate 65% disapproval rating of Trump on the economy , versus just 31.4% approval.
The numbers are even worse on inflation: 74.3% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of inflation, while just 22.6% approve.
This story has been updated.
Ben Werschkul is a Washington correspondent for Yahoo Finance.

articles.title_orig: Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87
articles.title_zh: Spanish PM Sánchez loses key housing crisis vote after eviction of woman, 87
articles.content_orig:
Spain's Congress has rejected a series of measures aimed at tackling the country's housing crisis, in a defeat for the government of Pedro Sánchez that increases pressure on him to call a snap election.
Lawmakers voted on two decree-laws presented by the government in response to nationwide protests that have followed the eviction of an 87-year-old woman, Maricarmen Abascal, from her home.
The decrees, which introduced a series of initiatives aimed at protecting tenants in the rental market, required parliamentary approval in order to remain in place.
MPs rejected the first decree by 178 votes to 172 and voted against the second by 184 to 166.
Hundreds of demonstrators had gathered outside Congress as the debate took place and there were angry scenes.
Protesters chanted "shame on you" and "your profits, our misery", after the results were announced.
The government's defeat underlines the fact that Sánchez, a Socialist, does not command a congressional majority and it has heightened speculation that he might call an early general election, which was not due until next summer.
Sources told Spanish media that the government would spend the weekend deciding its next step, and whether to dissolve parliament.
Sánchez's beleaguered government had already been mired in a series of scandals and judicial cases affecting his Socialist Party and close allies.
Abascal was evicted after she was unable to pay a sharp rent increase introduced by Urbagestión, the company that owned her flat in central Madrid.
Hundreds of protesters gathered to oppose the eviction last week and the case triggered a broader movement across the country demanding affordable rentals, which have soared in recent years.
The social backlash has seen Urbagestión negotiate the return of Abascal to her flat on a low rent. However, protests have continued, with people occupying squares in Madrid and other cities, pitching tents in squares and with a series of marches scheduled for this weekend.
The Sindicato de Inquilinas (Tenants' Union) activist association which has been co-ordinating protests, announced during the congressional debate that it was abandoning the tent protest in central Madrid. It said it wanted to "take the struggle to all the neighbourhoods, residential blocks and homes of Madrid, wherever there are rental increases, expulsions and abuses each day, and turn the energy of the last few days into a permanent organisation".
Protesters are also calling for a general strike over the housing crisis.
The left-wing coalition government responded to the social anger by hurriedly drawing up the two decree-laws in an effort to defuse the protests.
The first decree included the suspension of evictions of vulnerable tenants until 2030, a two-year extension to rental leases due to expire before 2028, tax increases for tourist apartments, and a restriction on the purchase of residential properties by what the government calls "vulture funds".
The second decree was more controversial, because it included the automatic renewal of rental contracts, a major demand of many on the left and the Sindicato de Inquilinas .
The conservative People's Party (PP) and far-right Vox had already said they would vote against both initiatives, leaving the minority government depending on the support of smaller nationalist parties in Catalonia and the Basque Country.
However, by the eve of the parliamentary session, the centre-right, pro-independence Together for Catalonia (JxCat) had signalled its opposition to both laws, condemning them to failure.
Friday's debate was fierce and at times angry, as supporters and opponents of the decrees clashed in Congress.
"I don't ask you, I beg you to be brave and consistent," Sánchez said, moments before the two votes took place. "Because they are not just ambitious measures, they are necessary".
He appealed to lawmakers "to put order and humanity into [the housing] market, because if we don't, it will bring down our society".
Social Affairs minister Pablo Bustinduy, of the Sumar alliance, the junior partner in the governing coalition, presented the debate in dramatic terms.
"Today is about defending an international oligarchy which is extracting the rent from salaries earned with the effort of working classes of this country in order to share it out with dividends and they don't even pay taxes in Spain," he said.
"Voting against these decrees today means defending the interests of this oligarchy and turning your back on your own people."
However, Miriam Nogueras, of JxCat, said the decrees had been hastily drawn up and lacked rigour.
She said the decrees "will allow [vulture] funds to keep buying, keep speculating and evictions to keep happening… these two decrees would provoke the opposite effect of what they aim to achieve."
The political right has argued that the government's attempts to intervene will frighten homeowners, causing them not to put their properties on the rental market and pushing prices up further.
Juan Bravo of the PP said "housing doesn't get cheaper with decrees, it gets cheaper with more homes".

articles.title_orig: Affordable Alternatives To Apple's AirPods Max
articles.title_zh: Affordable Alternatives To Apple's AirPods Max
articles.content_orig:
If you can live without deep iOS integration and the polished design, you could save hundreds.
We may receive a commission on purchases made from links.
If you're willing to pay for them, there's a lot to like about the AirPods Max . You get a dose of high-end design with deep iOS integration and smart features like Personalized Spatial Audio, Adaptive EQ, Live Translation, Adaptive Audio and Conversation Awareness. There's also lossless audio over USB-C, if you're into that sort of thing, but it's more common on spec sheets these days.
Of course, the main drawback with the AirPods Max has always been the price. At $549, the headphones rank among the most expensive sets we've reviewed. But if you're willing to give up some features, namely the tools that can only be used with Apple devices, you can save a significant sum without sacrificing too much performance.
Currently being tested for review.
At $200, the Space 2 Pro will cost you less than half of a pair of the AirPods Max 2. And yes, you will need to make some sacrifices to save that much dough. First and foremost, you'll give up the deep integration with iOS and Apple devices that the AirPods Max offers. You'll also have to forego the premium design for something that's still refined, but also decidedly plastic. If neither of those are dealbreakers, then there's plenty to like about the Space 2 Pro.
This most is Anker's first Soundcore headphones with its Thus AI chip inside. The component is responsible for active noise cancellation (ANC), voice quality (on both calls and for voice controls) and HearID customized sound. The ANC setup, which also utilizes eight sensors, does a decent job with human voices and constant noise sources. Voice quality is great, thanks in part to that chip and a six-microphone configuration, but you will notice some slight degradation when the system kicks in to block background noise. And the stock tuning offers crisp highs and deep low-end tone right out of the box.
The benefit of all that plastic is the Space 2 Pro is very light, so it's comfortable to wear for extended periods of time. These headphones also have intuitive physical controls that are reliable and easy to use instead of touch panels for swipes and taps. Multipoint Bluetooth and 30 hours of battery life (ANC on) are also on the spec sheet.
$359 is still a big chunk of change, but in the case of the second-gen QuietComfort Headphones, you're paying for Bose's noise-blocking prowess. The overall sound quality here is nice too, though the company's own Ultra model does better. On these "regular" QC headphones, you get Cinema Mode and Immersive Audio, the latter of which is the company's take on spatial sound. The QuietComfort Headphones are no slouch, and you'll be plenty pleased with the performance after saving nearly $200 over the AirPods Max 2.
Read our full review here.
At this point, you've likely seen someone wearing the AirPods Max 2 during a workout. Those headphones aren't a great choice for sweaty activities since the ear pads are made of "a breathable mesh textile." Beats headphones haven't been engineered to withstand sweat either, but they were also popular among gym goers and athletes. With the Beats 360 though, Apple finally has a set of fitness headphones in its lineup with IPX4 sweat resistance.
Since Beats is owned by Apple, you get a lot of the AirPods Max benefits here. Those include one-touch pairing, automatic switching between Apple devices on your iCloud account, Audio Sharing with compatible earbuds/headphones, Find My compatibility and hands-free access to Siri. The Beats 360 lasts for up to 12 hours longer than the AirPods Max 2 (ANC enabled) and there's the ability to swap out both the ear and headband cushions. Plus, Beats' affinity for bass will help keep your energy up during a workout, but it's not as overbearing as was on the company's early models.
If you want a good set of headphones for under $100, you have to make a lot of sacrifices. However, sound quality, battery life and comfort don't have to be on that list. With Audio-Technica's M20xBT, you get a classic design and the company's warm, inviting sound quality. 60-hour battery life is excellent and the headphones are lightweight and very comfy. What you won't find here is ANC, but basics like multipoint Bluetooth and optional wired use are still available.
When the comparison device is $549, a $299 set is significantly more affordable. In this case, that's the price of the Fender Mix: a set of noise-cancelling headphones that debuted just before CES. The new line of audio devices comes from Fender Audio, a collaboration of the Fender Corporation (of guitar fame) and Riffsound. The result is a cleverly designed set of headphones with a stored lossless Bluetooth dongle and replaceable battery. There's also a crisp, detailed quality to the sound that I really enjoyed. Plus, the company now has an app for settings changes, a key element that was missing during my review.
The five-way joystick controls are pleasant to use and 52 hours of battery life with ANC enabled is a big perk. Speaking of noise cancellation, the performance is respectable here, though it's not on the level of Bose and some others. Still, it's enough to block mild-to-moderate distractions.
Skullcandy Crusher 1080: Haptic bass is the main draw here, but the ANC performance and overall audio quality don't overcome the bulky, dated design.
JBL Live 780NC: This model is comfortable to wear with lots of features and solid active noise cancellation, but the overall sound quality is underwhelming and call quality isn't great either.
Sony WH-1000XM4C: This is still a solid set of headphones six years later, but Sony's reboot doesn't offer enough to justify the $300 price tag.
Sony WH-1000XM6: The best headphones you can buy right now will only save you $99 over the AirPods Max 2. That's not nothing, but it's also not enough in our book to name it an affordable alternative.
Bose QuietComfort Ultra Headphones (2nd gen): This is the best ANC performance you'll find, but at $449, these headphones don't fit the description of an affordable alternative either.
Sennheiser HDB 630: I really like the sound quality on these headphones, especially with the lossless audio capabilities. But at $500, these don't offer much savings over the AirPods Max 2.
Sennheiser Momentum 5: Sennheiser's well-rounded over-ear headphones are no slouch. The main issue that kept them off of this list is the $400 price.
Sonos Ace: Sonos' original headphones are now just $350 following the debut of the Ace Ultra. But unless you also have a Sonos soundbar, these aren't a very compelling alternative for everyday use.
When Engadget compiles buyer's guides like these, we initially draw on our decades of product review expertise. Throughout each year, we review well over 100 new devices, which gives us a solid foundation for selecting the best products that fit any given criteria. For this guide specifically, I was able to revisit recently reviewed devices as a refresher, re-familiarize myself with the products on my initial short list and make the best selections based on the affordable alternatives criteria. I write almost all of the headphone reviews at Engadget, and edit those I don't write, so I have a deep knowledge of this particular category.
We may update our selections as needed, after new products are announced and reviewed.

articles.title_orig: World News in Brief: Cycle of violence continues in Haiti, seafarer deaths off Somalia, food insecurity in the Middle East
articles.title_zh: World News in Brief: Cycle of violence continues in Haiti, seafarer deaths off Somalia, food insecurity in the Middle East
articles.content_orig:
Facebook Twitter Print Email
Haitians remain in the grip of lethal gang violence as it continues to “adapt and expand”, the UN’s top rights official, Volker Türk, said on Friday.
In an update to the Human Rights Council , the High Commissioner welcomed the first Gang Suppression Force operations, mandated by the UN Security Council .
These will help boost security in Haiti “but the Force remains far below the strength needed”, Mr. Türk insisted, in support of its “full, accelerated deployment” with human rights safeguards embedded.
At least 5,700 people have been confirmed killed or injured by gangs – or during operations against them – since 1 January, according to the UN human rights office, OHCHR .
Gang members have also kidnapped more than 230 people and raped at least 1,000 women and girls. The real figures are likely much higher, Mr. Türk said.
In his update, the High Commissioner for Human Rights also warned that “extortion, looting and destruction of property” are crippling economic activity in Haiti.
The “constant danger” prevents people from reaching schools, hospitals, and essential services, Mr. Türk stressed.
Three hijacked ships have been freed after months in captivity, but five seafarers died during the rescue of one of them, the head of the International Maritime Organization (IMO) has said.
IMO Secretary-General Arsenio Dominguez offered his condolences after the operation to free the HONOUR 25 in Somali waters on 29 September, in which several other crew members were seriously injured.
Mr. Dominguez said seafarers “should not have to lose their lives for the service they provide for the world”, and called for renewed resolve, targeted cooperation and the resources needed to stop piracy in the region.
The HONOUR 25 was one of three vessels released this week, along with the SEAMULL (also known as SIBU 1) and the MT EUREKA, all seized between April and August by pirates and armed robbers.
In total, 44 seafarers were freed and their governments are working to arrange their repatriation. Mr. Dominguez thanked Somalia's Government for its efforts, but noted that 22 seafarers remain captive aboard the ASANA.
He urged Governments to bring new initiatives, such as the proposed Group of Friends of Safety and Security of Shipping and Seafarers, to the IMO, and stressed the importance of the EUNAVFOR Aspides and Atalanta operations for maritime security in the region.
An additional 11.7 million women and girls in 28 countries could face food insecurity by the end of the year due to the escalating conflict in the Middle East and disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz.
These crises are driving up food prices and putting a strain on livelihoods and household resources, UN Women said in new analysis published on Friday.
Presenting the findings to journalists in Geneva, UN Women Deputy Executive Director Nyaradzayi Gumbonzvanda said the estimates are a potential scenario, not a forecast, and that the number is in addition to the 208 million women and girls who were already estimated to be food insecure or malnourished in these countries.
“Experience from past conflicts shows that when food is scarce, women often reduce the amount they eat or skip meals so that children and other family members can eat,” she said.
The greatest numbers of women and girls at risk are in populous countries, while South Sudan, Sudan, Haiti, Yemen and Palestine face the highest concentration of overlapping vulnerabilities.
UN Women recommends linking food and cash assistance to nutrition, protection, employment and agricultural services. Women should also have access to land, credit and productive resources.
The agency also highlighted the need for better collection of data that shows where food insecurity is worsening and who is eating less, losing income and carrying the heaviest burden of unpaid care work.

articles.title_orig: Protests shutter hundreds of French schools as violence flares
articles.title_zh: Protests shutter hundreds of French schools as violence flares
articles.content_orig:
What’s behind France’s school protests?
Hundreds of schools have been closed across France amid a student protest movement that has turned increasingly tumultuous.
At least 400 of France’s 3,700 high schools were closed on Friday, the Ministry of National Education said, with 560 reporting protests or disruptions. The demonstrations began at high schools in the Paris area last week, but they have spread nationwide and led to violent clashes with police.
On Friday, students across the country, many clad in masks, blockaded schools, lit fires in the streets, and faced off with police as they rallied against large class sizes and absent teachers .
“We are 35 per class, we don’t have enough chairs in classrooms, the one-hour lunch break [is too short] for everyone to get food,” 15-year-old Kesia told the Reuters news agency in the Paris suburb of Pantin before running off as the police used tear gas.
Fire damaged the entrances of two high schools in the capital, Leonard de Vinci in the south of the city and Gaston-Bachelard in the southeast, with the fire brigade called to extinguish the blazes.
Students waved placards reading “We have a future to build, not to endure.”
The school protest movement coincides with a public sector strike against the government’s budget plans, raising the pressure on President Emmanuel Macron before elections next year.
Approximately 2,000 people have been detained so far, the vast majority of whom are children, according to Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin.
Parents should be liable for damage caused by their children and “pay for repairs”, he told RTL.
Education Minister Edouard Geffray warned parents to “tell their children not to go” to the protests.
At least 170 students have been wounded, along with 65 school staff members, including 40 principals, he told BFMTV. More than 100 high schools have sustained “severe damage”.
“What matters now is ensuring our children are no longer out on the streets, because they are in danger,” Geffray declared.
Rights group Amnesty International wrote on social media that “the images of high school students being assaulted by law enforcement are extremely alarming”.
“Many are minors, children,” the organisation said. “They must be protected, not beaten with batons.”
Lola, a 16-year-old speaking to the AFP news agency in the western city of Rennes, condemned what she described as police violence while standing outside Jean-Mace high school.
“It makes us even angrier – the police have no right to hit us or use tear gas on us,” Lola said.
The government has accused the hard-left France Unbowed (LFI) party of commandeering the movement. Senior LFI official Manuel Bompard dismissed the assertion as a “conspiracy theory”.
In an effort to quell tensions, Geffray said he planned to meet on Friday with education unions and student associations to find room for dialogue.

articles.title_orig: Gino’s Pizza Place owner is old guard in a new world
articles.title_zh: Gino’s Pizza Place owner is old guard in a new world
articles.content_orig:
Gino has proudly served the Tonawanda community from 351 Fries Road since opening his doors in 1983.
Now in his fourth decade of making pizza at his eponymous restaurant in Tonawanda, Gino Pinzone is a part of the old guard who made Buffalo pizza a thing. At seventy years old, he still gets behind the counter of Gino’s Pizza Place at 9 a.m. to make dough, prep sauce, and mentor a new generation of employees.
You’ve been a fixture in the local food scene for decades. Where did that passion for cooking begin?
Everything started back in Sicily. My mother had eleven children, so she worked at home day and night, night and day, constantly cooking for fourteen people. I’m number eight, so I did a lot of helping, making everything you could possibly make at home. I still do it for myself today. I learned everything from her.
Did she teach you to bake?
In those days, we really could not afford meat. Bread was everything. Chinese people use rice. Mexicans use tortilla shells. We were heavy on bread. When it came out of the oven, it was a treat just to put extra virgin olive oil and black pepper on it. That was it.
How did you end up owning a pizzeria?
I went to Buffalo State for Industrial Arts; I was going to be a teacher. But in 1978, my older brother opened a pizzeria and asked me and my brother Frank to work for him. I liked it a lot. I never finished my master's degree in teaching because I was doing okay making pizzas with my brother! I opened my first solo place in November 1983, and here I am today.
What do you love the most?
My employees. Some started as high school students from across the street. They start folding boxes and then, little by little, I teach them how to do a few things here and there. They might go away for college, but they always come back. It’s rewarding. Take care of the employees because the employees will always take care of you. And that’s what they do. I trust them, and they do a great job.
It sounds almost like a family atmosphere .
I get kids coming in who might be a little quiet or shy. Their parents ask if I can hire them, to get them out of their bedrooms and away from the video games. Next thing you know, they’re hopping around and working and loving it. I tell them, “You’re learning a skill.”
It’s not just about making pizzas but also learning how to get around a restaurant. You need to do dishes, you need to cut celery, you need to do this... Even if they graduate and get a degree, they can go anywhere in the world and work in a pizzeria because they know how a kitchen moves.
Many of the restaurant’s Instagram reels feature you. Do you enjoy being in the spotlight?
[Laughs] My son Phil does all that! He puts the camera in my face and says, “Dad, we’re introducing eggplant pizza today.” I always tell him, “Phil, I’m not doing a second take.” Whatever comes out of me, comes out. We did one video recently that had 20,000 viewers. People come in now just because they want to see me and talk to me.
Why have you never expanded to a second location?
I want to be totally responsible for everything that comes out of the place. I do all the prep work. I’m there from 9 a.m. to 1 p.m. every day. On Fridays, I’m there until dinner is over. On Sundays, I’m there until the Bills game is over.  Nobody does it like the owner. It’s hard to train somebody to do things the way I do. Nowadays, people open five places and there’s no personal feeling.
And after forty years, most people would be taking it easy. What keeps you coming back every morning?
It’s not the money. It’s the DNA of a pizza guy in me. I see regulars who came in as kids now bringing their own grandkids in and putting them up on my counter. Why would I walk away? It makes it all worthwhile.

articles.title_orig: A small Texas town stopped Trump’s border wall construction – for now
articles.title_zh: A small Texas town stopped Trump’s border wall construction – for now
articles.content_orig:
As they had in the past, San Ygnacio residents banded together to stop a development threatening their town
This story was co-published and supported by the journalism non-profit the Economic Hardship Reporting Project .
Joel Ruiz pointed his cane toward a long piece of metal lying in the dirt. Unwanted construction crews had left it behind on his riverfront property where he has lived and run a small fishing business for decades in San Ygnacio, Texas .
At 90, Ruiz still tends the land. But in July, heavy machinery gouged the earth where mesquite and dense brush once grew. A steel barricade of 30ft-high bars was erected across the riverfront, including on his property just across the Rio Grande from Mexico.
For months, Ruiz and a handful of other San Ygnacio residents have been trying to halt the construction of a federal border wall in their Mexican American town of roughly 400 people . They’ve blocked bulldozers, been arrested, unearthed 75-year-old land records and filed lawsuits challenging the federal government’s authority to build here. Even though residents say nearly all the riverfront land in the county is privately owned, the government is building on it anyway, claiming a decades-old right.
While they have stopped construction on the disputed land for now – a verbal concession, not a court order – the reprieve is precarious: the lawsuits are unresolved, the federal money set aside for construction remains in place and residents know the crews could be back. But they are drawing on the memory of a town that rose up against the government once before.
“This little spot is all we have,” said Elsa Hull, who owns property downriver with her two daughters. “But [residents] fought the federal government before and won – and we can do it again.”
Founded along the Rio Grande in 1830, San Ygnacio grew from a cluster of ranches into a small border town. Today, its plaza is still lined with homes made of sandstone quarried from the riverbank. The town sits in Zapata county , where roughly 38% of residents live below the poverty line and the median household income is about $39,000. Many work in healthcare, schools, food service and ranching. The border patrol is a major regional employer : its sector in Laredo employs about 3,025 people.
The construction is part of the Trump administration’s renewed border-wall push – a roughly $46.5bn expansion funded by what is known as the One Big Beautiful Bill Act. San Ygnacio is located in one of the stretches where that money is now hitting the ground – and it’s going up as the number of border apprehensions is dropping drastically. Ruiz said he rarely sees anyone crossing this stretch of river any more.
The Rio Grande is also San Ygnacio’s sole source of drinking water, and the wall is being built in its floodplain. To expedite construction, the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) waived 30 federal laws – among them the Clean Water Act and the National Environmental Policy Act, eliminating the environmental review that would normally accompany a project of this scale. (The DHS did not respond to the Guardian’s request for comment.)
To fill that gap, the Laredo-based Rio Grande International Study Center (RGISC) commissioned its own. The assessment warned that the wall and buoy system along and in the Rio Grande would worsen flooding – and, in places, fail outright.
“This is life or death for us,” said Tricia Cortez, the center’s executive director. A breach of the wall system, she warned, would be sudden and catastrophic – homes destroyed, lives endangered. “The wall will straitjacket the river, forcing flood waters to rise and move faster.”
Construction in San Ygnacio had begun without notice. Residents watched what they called a “man camp” rise at its edge and sensed something was coming. At a June community meeting to discuss other business, word began spreading through the back of the room: contractors were clearing land along the riverbank. Several residents hurried down and confronted the equipment operators, telling them they were on private property.
Hull spent 25 years as an environmental investigator for the Texas commission on environmental quality . She recalled how she would watch deer, bobcats, coyotes and sunsets over the river from a bench beneath a tree on the bluff. Border construction has since knocked the tree down and smashed the bench.
“Every part of my life is intertwined with the Rio Grande,” Hull said. “To me this river is sacred.”
When contractors arrived near Ruiz’s home and RV park in June, he invited Hull and her friend to see the damage done. Crews had razed trees and severed an irrigation line. Before leaving for an appointment, Ruiz signed a paper authorizing Hull and her friend to stay and watch the property.
Two contractor trucks slipped through the gate. Hull said one worker repeatedly flashed a card marked “CBP” – presumably Customs and Border Protection. Then she noticed Southwest Valley Constructors identification on his vest.
“You’re not CBP,” Hull recalled telling him. When another truck approached, Hull drove her car across the entrance. More trucks arrived, followed by sheriff’s deputies, state troopers and border patrol agents.
“We were just surrounded by all these men,” Hull said.
Hull pulled up the county appraisal map and argued the crews were on Ruiz’s property. A deputy insisted the land was federal. Finally, Hull put her water bottle on the hood of her car and sat down.
“Fuck it,” she said. “Arrest me.” They did.
On 14 August, Hull returned, carrying a flag that read “Keep Our River Free” on one side and “Walls and Buoys Kill” on the other. When a sheriff’s deputy called to her from across a fence, she thought he wanted to talk. Instead, she was handcuffed and arrested again.
San Ygnacio had fought the federal government for this land once before – and won. When government contractors insisted the land was federal, Frank “Chip” Briscoe, an architectural conservator, started digging through county records.
The trail led back to the early 1950s, when the government built the Falcon dam. Its reservoir submerged historic ranch communities and Indigenous sites along the river, and San Ygnacio was scheduled to be condemned and cleared for the reservoir, too. But residents refused to accept it. In 1951, more than 200 people signed a petition, organized by local veterans and civic leaders, opposing the measure. It worked: the government carved San Ygnacio out of the condemnation, the one stretch along the river bend spared from the reservoir. Seventy years later, the town is invoking that same exclusion again.
Briscoe and attorney Ricardo de Anda searched subsequent property records and still found no evidence that the federal government had later acquired the excluded land. The documents gave De Anda something concrete to act on. In mid-June, he met with the US army corps of engineers on Ruiz’s behalf, arguing the crews had no legal grounds to build on the disputed property.
When construction continued, De Anda sent a warning letter and filed two lawsuits against the federal government, alleging it took private property in violation of the fifth amendment . Two more landowners are preparing to sue, and De Anda plans to sue the contractor, Southwest Valley Constructors, in state court. Landowners filed criminal trespass complaints, while about a dozen residents pressed local officials to intervene.
About a month later, according to De Anda, the county attorney arranged a meeting with contractors and federal officials.
“They agreed to stop,” he said, and the crews pulled back – for now.
For De Anda, stopping construction is only part of the plan. “Our strategy is to affect the national consciousness,” he said. The rest is a matter of time. Every day they hold the line – with their bodies, their deeds, their lawsuits – buys more of it. They are looking toward the midterms, hoping a change in Congress could give them another opening. They are betting they can outlast

articles.title_zh: Gold & The Battalion Approved to Transition to World Class
articles.content_orig:
REBROADCAST: Texas Marching Classic
Massive drum corps news just dropped.
DCI Open Class veterans Gold and The Battalion have both been approved to transition into the World Class beginning with the 2027 DCI Summer Tour.
All of the Bands Competing at the 2027 Texas Marching Classic 🤠   | BOA Weekend Watch Guide, Oct. 3 🗓️   | Troopers Announce DCI 2027 Show Title 👀   | Recent Marching Headlines You May Have Missed 🔥   | WATCH LIVE on October 17: Texas Marching Classic 🤠
After a successful vote by DCI's member organizations in addition to a multi-year examination of the organizations' finances and operations, both Gold and The Battalion are excited to endeavor on a new adventure in their new class.
A recent success story of the transition from Open Class to World Class is Spartans, which just completed its first full season as a DCI World Class member with their show, 'On the World Stage.'
Here's what the two ensembles had to say to DCI about the move:
“This is a culmination of everything we’ve been building over the last 12 years. For our staff and members, there’s definitely excitement, but I think it will mostly feel like a natural next step, because we’ve always seen ourselves as headed in this direction. We’ve been incredibly honored by the new fans we’ve met on the road as our tours have grown longer each year. We’re excited to grow that community as we take this step.” - Tyler Hess, director of The Battalion
“Moving into World Class is a big moment for Gold. It’s something we’ve been working toward for a long time, even if it wasn’t always the immediate goal in front of us. We’ve always worked hard to make drum corps accessible and to create a place where members can grow as performers and as people. That remains important to us regardless of what classification we compete in.” - Kevin Valentine, executive director of Gold
To read DCI's full press release, click here.
The Battalion had a breakout year, earning the silver medal at DCI Open Class World Championships (81.500) and 20th at DCI World Championship Semifinals (79.225).
Gold finished out the 2026 DCI season placing third at DCI Open Class World Championships (80.300) and 22nd at DCI World Championship Semifinals (77.975).

articles.title_orig: The 7-year-old Nvidia Shield TV is now $100 more expensive due to AI
articles.title_zh: The 7-year-old Nvidia Shield TV is now $100 more expensive due to AI
articles.content_orig:
The era of generative AI has upended technology supply chains, and there is one ironclad rule in 2026: If it has memory or storage, it’s getting more expensive. Even devices with years-old tech inside are still apparently subject to that unwritten rule. Nvidia has just announced that the Shield TV Pro is getting $100 more expensive, effective immediately.
The most recent version of the Shield streaming box debuted in 2019, running Android TV with AI upscaling and hardware decoding for almost any type of media. While it ran an aging Tegra X1+ processor, that was (and still is) fast for a TV media streamer. The device launched at $199.99, with a non-Pro variant at $149.99. The non-Pro Shield has since been discontinued, but the Shield TV Pro lives on at the new $299.99 price.
Nvidia has confirmed that you can blame AI for the higher Shield TV pricing. “Starting October 2, SHIELD Pro will be priced at $299. The cost of components, including memory, has increased substantially across the industry,” a spokesperson told Ars.
When we talked to Nvidia’s Andrew Bell earlier this year, he framed the Shield as a passion project , but it looks like passion projects still have to pay the bills at Nvidia. In that interview, Bell explained that Nvidia still actively manufactures the Shield and sells every unit it makes. Without a stockpile of pre-AI hardware to sell, new Shield TV units are subject to the same supply chain constraints as today’s smartphones and computers.
Nvidia isn’t a victim here, though. As a key player in AI hyperscaling, the company is more responsible than most for the sky-high cost of components. It has also become one of the most valuable firms in the world thanks to its market-leading AI accelerators and GPUs. As a consequence, we’re seeing new products launch at higher prices than their predecessors, and many end up getting more expensive during their lifetimes. Game consoles have been particularly affected, with Nintendo , Microsoft , and Sony all bumping the prices of their current-gen hardware. The PS5 Pro, for example, has gone from $699.99 at launch in 2024 to $899.99 today.
Stock of the Shield TV Pro has been slim for the last few months, probably because it became too expensive to manufacture new units with component prices rising so quickly. At $300, it will make sense for Nvidia to churn out more devices. However, this higher price will cause an already niche set-top box to be even less appealing to people who just want to stream Netflix.
Unless you need the Shield’s extensive codec support or Plex server capability, it makes more sense to get a cheaper streamer. The Shield is still out of stock on Nvidia’s store , but it’s available at the new price from Best Buy .

articles.title_orig: A Different World Season 2: Sequel Series Is Officially Renewed
articles.title_zh: A Different World Season 2: Sequel Series Is Officially Renewed
articles.content_orig:
A new generation of Hillman College students arrived on campus in Season 1 of A Different World , and soon, their education will continue. The sequel series from showrunner and executive producer Felicia Pride has officially been renewed for Season 2.
“We are beyond excited to return to Hillman and continue to tell meaningful and heartfelt stories that resonate across generations. I am thrilled for our brilliant cast and our hardworking crew,” Pride exclusively tells Tudum. “It's so validating to be bolstered by our amazing audience.”
A Different World Season 1 launched on Sept. 24 with honors, making the Netflix English TV Top 10 list. “It’s because of our incredible fans that we've received such a swift Season 2 pickup! You all have watched, rewatched, posted about, created content around, and hosted events for our show. Your support, passion, and love mean the absolute world,” Pride says. “From the passionate pleas for their favorite ’ships to feeling seen by a particular character to uncovering well-laid Easter eggs , the conversations fans have been having are so rich and joyful. And I love that audiences are watching it together — parents with children, college friends, and extended family — all enjoying it in community.”
Executive producer and director Debbie Allen can’t wait for the next chapter of A Different World . “Yay! Hallelujah! The people and Netflix have spoken. A Different World brought something everybody needed: joy, romance, relevance, authenticity, and HEART,” she says. “Thank you for getting us into the Top 10 worldwide ! And now, gear up! We’re coming back at you with Season 2!”
Looking ahead, Pride promises “more Hillman, more college life, more friendship, more romance, more Black joy, and more HBCU greatness” in A Different World Season 2. You can also expect answers to some of your most burning questions following Deborah Wayne’s (Maleah Joi Moon) first year at Hillman. “Of course, we left Season 1 with quite a few cliffhangers that we must address in Season 2,” says Pride.
While you wait for classes to reconvene, study up on everything there is to know about A Different World ’s renewal and check back here for more news as it’s announced.
After transformative summers, Deborah and her Hillman classmates return to campus for sophomore year with a “new year, new me” attitude, only to find themselves faced with past decisions, uncertain futures, new loves and friendships, and deeper questions of purpose … all while, of course, getting themselves into a whole lot of new mess.
The show has only just been renewed for another school year, so there’s no release date yet. Keep checking back here for major updates coming from campus.
A lot! The sequel series follows Deborah, the youngest child of Dwayne Wayne (Kadeem Hardison) and Whitley Gilbert (Jasmine Guy), as she enters her first year at Hillman College. In the shadow of her well-meaning but sometimes overbearing parents, Deborah attempts to build her own legacy at the HBCU. As she spreads her wings as a young adult, Debo builds deep bonds with fellow Hillmanites — Rashida (Alijah Kai), Hazel (Kennedi Reece), Amir (Jordan Aaron Hall), and Kojo (Chibuikem Uche) — all of whom navigate their own academic and interpersonal struggles. Deborah also rekindles a romance with a special someone from her past, football superstar Shaquille (Cornell Young IV ), and explores a new connection with upperclassman Ellington (Vincent Jamal Hooper).
But there’s more to the sequel series than the new generation. Beloved characters from the original series return as parents, professors, administrators, and esteemed alumni to help dig Hillman out of a financial hole and prove that you never fully graduate from personal drama. For a complete breakdown of all the messiness that ensues in A Different World Season 1, including cast insights on relationship cliffhangers, check out Tudum’s ending explainer .
Of course, you could always run it back and rewatch Season 1 or return to the OG series to relive the glory days of your favorite Hillman alums. And dive deeper into all the connections between old-school and new with Pride in the 10 Nostalgic Things You Might’ve Missed in A Different World video below. You can also check out student life on other campuses with Tudum’s list of college series and movies . Or if Debo’s dating complications have left you craving more romantic turmoil, check out these movies and shows centered on love triangles .
A freshman and her ride-or-die crew juggle school, romantic drama and family legacy at a historically Black college.

articles.title_orig: Pixel 10a gets a $100 price hike, now starting at $599
articles.title_zh: Pixel 10a gets a $100 price hike, now starting at $599
articles.content_orig:
Google has quietly raised the price of its mid-range Pixel 10a by $100, giving the device a starting price of $599.
Effective as of today at the Google Store, Pixel 10a has jumped from $499 to $599. The reason is obvious, of course, with the current skyrocketing costs of components such as memory. Google has not officially commented on the price hike yet, though.
This follows Google issuing a price increas e to each of its new Pixel 11 devices compared to the prior generation.
When Google confirmed the Pixel 11 would be more expensive, the company said that this would eventually impact “in-market Pixel phones” which, at the time, we speculated could include Pixel 10a.
The 128GB base Pixel 10a is $599 as of today, with the 256GB model at $699. The updated prices have already kicked in at Amazon and Best Buy , and Google Store now shows Pixel 10a at $849 in Canada, £599 in the UK, and €649 in Europe.
However, this could be fine IF it means the 11a will come at the same $599 price and with Tensor G6 and PixelSnap magnets.
Hopefully street price for those wanting to buy a 10a soon won't change much.
In our review of Pixel 10a , we called the device a “well-rounded experience” for its $499 price, but a $100 jump certainly makes that a tougher conversation, especially considering Google’s mid-ranger is at this point using a two-generation-old chipset in its Tensor G4. But, of course, Google is far from alone here. Just this week, Samsung also issued price hikes across the Galaxy lineup including flagship and mid-range devices alike.
AI is just great isn’t it?
